thesis_card.viewer_belief: 小冰期是一场五百年的漫长绝望，普通人只能听天由命，活下来靠的是运气或者住在气候更温暖的地方
thesis_card.truth: 同一场饥荒里，有备荒储粮制度的地方和没有的地方，人口损失差出了几乎一半——死亡率的高低不是天气决定的，是组织决定的。劳动力稀缺后的供需反转也不是自动发生的，哪里有足够强的领主或法律压制，哪里的工资就被压住了；反转只在劳动力冲击够大、且制度管控够弱的地方才真正出现。
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 小冰期杀死的不是最冷地方的人，而是没有组织的人
thesis_card.ending_landing: 今天我们讨论气候韧性，总说技术和钱，但天明大饥荒告诉我们：同一片天空下，一纸储粮制度的差距，就是生与死的差距。历史上最能帮人活下来的，从来不是运气，而是提前建好的那一套互相兜底的制度。
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论：①普通社区在制度崩解中仍维持体面与秩序；②灾难后的供需反转为幸存者打开了祖辈从未有过的空间；③宏观事件是被一屋一田具体经历的。本题论点：①和②完全保留（体面峰值用夏蒙尼集体墓、供需反转用1349年劳工法令压不住工资），③保留并扩展为'以王国尺度被记住却在一屋一田间被经历'。核心增补：制度与组织（备荒义仓、济贫法、国家赈济）是比个人适应更关键的生存变量——这是小冰期五百年跨度才能讲清楚的命题，单一疫病事件（黑死病）讲不出来。
thesis_card.contrast: 揭示：观众知道小冰期寒冷、知道很多人死了，但不知道'同样的天气、有组织的地方死得少、没组织的地方死得多'这个结构性差异；也不知道供需反转不是自动的，被制度压制的地方（如立法限薪）反转就不发生。
thesis_card.double_standard: 同一场天明大饥荒（1782-88），日本东北弘前藩死亡接近半数、九州几乎无饥荒痕迹；同一个1690年代寒冷期，芬兰死1/3人口、荷兰因波罗的海粮食贸易体系受损最轻。
thesis_card.boundary: 论点主要适用于饥荒型灾害（粮食短缺可通过储备、贸易、替代作物缓解），对瘟疫（病原体传播逻辑不同，隔离和医疗比粮食储备更关键）、火山直接伤亡（如坦博拉1815年火山碎屑流）的解释力有限。也不适用于规模极小、完全孤立、没有任何贸易或互助网络的社区。

facts.slot: 小冰期时间范围与成因
facts.content: 小冰期通行时间范围约1300-1850年，北半球平均降温不到1°C（相对20世纪晚期）。成因：密集火山喷发（1257年萨马拉斯火山VEI 7级、1268/1275/1284三连发、1452/53年夸埃火山）+ 太阳活动四个大极小期（沃尔夫、斯波勒、蒙德1645-1715、道尔顿）
facts.source: 同行评审：NASA划定三个最冷段、IPCC第三次评估报告、火山喷发与太阳黑子数据

facts.content: 1315年春起欧洲北部暴雨连绵，英格兰粮价春季到仲夏翻倍；诺福克郡谷物从每夸特5先令涨到20先令（涨3倍）；洛林小麦涨320%
1315年8月10日，英格兰国王爱德华二世路过圣奥尔本斯，国王的随从都买不到面包
城市死亡率估计10-25%；英格兰南部10-15%；法国北部约10%；直到1322-1325年才恢复
芬兰大饥荒（1695-97）两年内饿死全国约1/3人口（约15万/50万）。人们吃树皮面包；1696年出现痢疾、斑疹伤寒。芬兰史称'大死之年'（Suuret kuolonvuodet）
苏格兰'七年荒年'（Seven Ill Years，1695-1699）人口损失10-15%。这场饥荒逼出了达连计划——苏格兰举全国约1/5资本去巴拿马地峡建殖民地，1698-1700年惨败（3000殖民者仅1000生还），直接压垮苏格兰财政，成为1707年苏格兰与英格兰合并的关键推手
1783年6月8日冰岛拉基裂隙喷发，持续8个月：14立方公里熔岩、约1.2亿吨二氧化硫。氟污染牧草→冰岛牲畜五到八成死于氟中毒，随后'雾难'饥荒夺走约9000-10000人（全国人口的1/5到1/4）。同年日本浅间山喷发+冷夏→天明大饥荒，奥羽地区约50万人死亡
1816年（坦博拉火山次年）：纽约、缅因6月6日下雪，魁北克积雪近一英尺；宾夕法尼亚河流8月结冰；弗吉尼亚8月20-21日霜冻；佛蒙特人称'一千八百年，冻死了'（Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death）。燕麦价格从每桶12美分飙到92美分
facts.source: 一手：当时报纸与日记；纽约震教徒教区尼古拉斯·贝内特逐日记录

facts.slot: 天明vs天保饥荒死亡率与出逃率同步
facts.content: 天明（1780年代）和天保（1830年代）两次饥荒期间，死亡率和出逃率同步上升，米价剧烈波动，人口在这两次饥荒中出现显著下降
facts.source: Xavier Data人口与家庭历史项目1708-1870年数据

facts.content: 天明大饥荒期间，九州地区史料里几乎找不到天明饥荒或天保饥荒的死亡痕迹
facts.source: The three major famines of Japanese history. Alan Macfarlane

facts.content: 土豆16世纪中叶到欧洲，长期被当猪食，法国1748年甚至立法禁止种植（时人相信它致麻风）。转折在小冰期饥荒年代：普鲁士腓特烈大帝1744年把土豆塞进军队口粮；1774年饥荒时下令全国推广种植、免费发薯种。到1815年土豆已成北欧主粮之一
facts.source: 官方档案+联合国粮农组织（FAO）

facts.content: 法国药剂师帕蒙蒂埃七年战争中被普鲁士俘虏，靠土豆活命，回国后毕生推广：1772年巴黎医学院宣告土豆可食；他在巴黎西郊种薯田，白天设岗、晚上撤岗任人来偷；向路易十六献上土豆花
facts.source: 一手：法国医学院档案、帕蒙蒂埃生平记录

facts.content: 芬兰1695-97年大饥荒期间，人们吃树皮面包、野蕨和杂草

facts.slot: 荷兰波罗的海粮食贸易
facts.content: 1590年代全欧大饥荒中，荷兰受损最轻——阿姆斯特丹的波罗的海粮食贸易体系保证了供应
近代早期英格兰1598年伊丽莎白《济贫法》被研究者解读为对小冰期气候变化和饥荒危机的制度性适应，体现了不同社会阶层之间的合作与团结机制
德语区和斯堪的纳维亚的瓷砖蓄热炉（Kachelofen），火砖砌成迷宫式烟道，燃料利用率80-90%（敞口壁炉只有10-15%），烧一两个小时、熄火后还能散热6-12小时。18世纪木材短缺严重到多国政府出资改进炉型
俄罗斯大炉（Russian stove）15世纪成熟，一两吨重的砖砌巨物立在木屋中央，烟气走'膝盖'形迂回烟道；炉顶就是全家的床——冬天一家老小睡在炉子上
床周挂帐（把床变成保暖帐篷）；长柄铜'暖床炉'（warming pan）睡前烘被；壁炉里烧热的砖块和皂石裹布暖脚；教堂里信众自带'脚炉'（foot stove）熬过一小时布道；冬天全家挤一张床；厨房兼作冬季全家起居室，客厅卧室整个冬天关门弃用
1349年英格兰《劳工法令》立法压制工资上涨，但'立法改变不了基本算术'——人少地多，工资在罚单的缝隙里上涨。长期后果：租金货币化与身份松动，1381年农民起义
夏蒙尼集体墓考古细节：48人，过半儿童，仍按头脚朝向安放。研究者震撼的不是混乱，而是体面
facts.source: 考古/实物：《过去的气候》期刊（Climate of the Past）2022年综述

facts.content: 1600-1650年间，仅法国夏蒙尼山谷就有至少6个村庄被推进的冰川夷平；1642年夏蒙尼官员记录冰川'每日推进'、冰雪卷走房屋牲畜；1644年布瓦冰川几乎堵死整个山谷
facts.source: 一手：地方官档案，引自《过去的气候》期刊2022年综述

facts.content: 泰晤士河冰冻集市1608年首次成规模；最盛的是1683-84年——河面封冻约两个月、冰层厚约28厘米，河上搭起两条'商铺街'：酒馆、理发店、咖啡摊、烤全牛、斗熊、木偶戏。日记作家约翰·伊夫林写道：'河上像一场狂欢的酒神节，陆上却是严苛的天罚'
1795年1月23日，荷兰登海尔德外海封冻，法国第8骠骑兵团的马蹄裹着布、踏着冰面突袭，一枪未发俘虏了被冻住的荷兰舰队14艘战舰、850门炮——军事史上罕见的'骑兵俘获舰队'
1709年可能是欧洲500年来最冷的冬天：葡萄酒在酒窖里冻结、树木冻裂、北海大片封冻。法国当年死于饥饿与营养不良者估计约50万人
facts.source: 一手记录+估计：勒华拉杜里学派口径
facts.method: 法国各来源估计值有出入，取勒华拉杜里学派约50万的口径

facts.content: 格陵兰诺斯人985年起建两个殖民点，小冰期来临后：海冰围困港口、牧草减产、贸易线被黑死病打断。西殖民点约1350年荒废；东殖民点撑到15世纪中叶——最后书面记录是1408年赫瓦尔塞教堂的一场婚礼，最晚放射性碳定年为1430±15年。同一片冰天雪地里，因纽特人靠皮划艇、鱼叉、海豹皮服活得很好
1637-1643年'崇祯大旱'可能是中国近500年最严重的干旱。1639年《益都县志》：'自正月不雨至于六月，七月大蝗，岁大饥，人相食，流民载道。'1640年山东48个州县记'人相食'。旱灾带蝗灾，山西又暴发大鼠疫——华北三省死亡总数至少千万级
树轮与模型显示1650年前后气温已回升到历史均值——只差六年，明朝没熬过去

气候史学家贝林格研究显示，欧洲猎巫高峰（1560-74、1583-89、1623-30、1678-98）与极端寒冷期高度重合。1562年维森施泰格一场冰雹后烧死63名'女巫'；1626年5月弗兰肯地区反常霜冻，蔡尔编年史家记暴民质问：'为什么当局还容忍那些糟蹋收成的巫师？'统计学上，气温每降一个标准差，猎巫审判数上升约0.2个标准差。但2017年《经济学杂志》对21国4.3万例审判的研究认为宗教竞争解释力更强，气候说被批'过度简化'
facts.source: 同行评审（两方争论都列出）

facts.content: 瑞士菲施村民从17世纪中叶起每年列队上山，祈求冰川别再吞他们的牧场。这套仪式沿用三百多年，直到21世纪冰川因气候变暖加速消融——2012年，当地主教向梵蒂冈申请把祷词反过来，改为祈求冰川别消失，获批

thesis_check.note: 论点'小冰期杀死的不是最冷地方的人，而是没有组织的人'由以下事实撑住：F07（同一场天明大饥荒，日本东北死亡约50万、九州无饥荒痕迹）、F09+F10（死亡率与出逃率同步上升vs九州无痕迹，支撑'有组织vs没组织'的对照）、F14（荷兰因波罗的海粮食贸易体系受损最轻）、F15（英格兰1598济贫法作为制度性适应）、F19（劳动力稀缺后供需反转不是自动的，立法压制的地方工资被压住）。没有与论点直接相反的事实。需注意的边界：论点主要适用于饥荒型灾害，对瘟疫（F25格陵兰诺斯人消失有贸易崩溃+适应速度因素，不只是组织）解释力较弱，已在thesis_card.boundary中说明。

modules.retention_role: scene_entry：进入1348年梅西纳港的具体现场，用编年史家悬念记录打开LOOP01
modules.reason: 小冰期题材有同样完整的开场锚点：1348年6月梅西纳港、编年史家Michele da Piazza记录'水手带来别的东西'。开场画面换成梅西纳港的季节与商船，编年史家视角保持不变，悬念句'别的东西'指向黑死病（小冰期最致命的单一事件），完全支撑PK01（premise_reveal强度70）。

modules.retention_role: premise_hook：史料宣言+四个子问题挂出主悬念，打开LOOP02
modules.reason: 小冰期证据比原片更丰富：四类证据可改为'庄园法庭记录、主教登记、树轮年代、考古墓地'，标题问句'如何活下来'拆成四个子问题：①寒冷如何传导成饥荒②谁活下来谁没有③为何有的地方全灭有的地方无事④改变了什么。PK02（information_reveal强度75）用'不是传说而是逐行记录在册'完成。

modules.retention_role: world_before_context：建立灾前基线，埋下heriot（葬礼税）伏笔，打开LOOP06
modules.reason: 小冰期版本：人口与资源压力基线（英格兰400-500万人口、可耕地达极限）、此前创伤（1315-1322大饥荒F02、1319牲畜大疫）、庄园制度运作（农民依附于庄园、劳役换土地）、heriot（葬礼税）制度细节、对善终的信仰要求（临终圣礼）。PK03（information_reveal强度70）用'琐碎的葬礼税让今天的历史学家能够数清死者'完成伏笔。

modules.retention_role: knowledge_contrast：时代认知vs现代科学的双镜头对照，打开LOOP04（明示不闭合）
modules.reason: 小冰期完美适配：时代认知（巴黎大学1348年星象-瘴气解释+教会神罚解释）、现代科学（从遗骸重建鼠疫耶尔森菌基因组F01、火山喷发与太阳活动数据F01）、学界争议（传播机制：跳蚤vs人际）、视角回落到当事人只能看见的表象世界。PK04（information_reveal强度75）用现代基因组证据完成。

modules.retention_role: arrival_mechanism：展示灾难进入社区的通道，拦截失败
modules.reason: 小冰期用寒冷的传播机制：商路扩散（1348年从梅西纳沿商路蔓延一年）、村庄与外界的连接网（集市、磨坊、教堂、法庭的日常出行）、拦截尝试（记录在案但全部失败）。PK05（information_reveal强度65）用'It didn't work.'两个字落下前现代拦截的宿命。增补F22（冰冻集市）和F23（骑兵俘虏舰队）作为'异常'钩子：寒冷到什么程度。

modules.retention_role: stakes_immersion：让观众与一个普通家庭同处一室，看清环境压力如何渗透进日常生活

analysis_original.core_dilemma: 灾难来临时，一个普通村庄面对的核心两难：是把有限的粮食储备用来救济最穷的租户（可能让整个村子撑不过冬天），还是优先保证有劳动力的家庭（让最弱的先死）？有义仓的藩选择了前者，没有义仓的藩连选择的机会都没有。
analysis_original.comment_question: If you lived in a medieval village during the Little Ice Age, would you rather have: (A) A slightly warmer climate but no grain storage system, or (B) A colder climate but a lord who kept a community granary?

hook.contract: 钩子类型：documentary_scene_entry_with_evidence_manifesto_and_question_barrage；第一个刺激：24.3秒（编年史家悬念记录）；第一个甜头：31.2秒（史料宣言'不是传说而是逐行记录在册'）；开场窗口：0-150秒

candidates.text: 1348年6月，意大利南部港口梅西纳（Messina），季节正值初夏，商船从东方归来。编年史家Michele da Piazza记下了一笔：这些水手带来了'别的东西'（something else）。这个'别的东西'会在接下来一年里沿着商路蔓延整个欧洲，改写一代人的命运。但这不是某一个村庄的故事——这是大多数人真实生活的那种村庄：同一个洗礼池、同一场婚礼、同一片墓地。
1695年，芬兰的冬天冷到树木冻裂。到1697年，全国约三分之一的人口——15万人——死于饥荒。同一个十年，苏格兰损失了10-15%的人口，这场饥荒直接压垮了苏格兰的财政，逼出了1707年与英格兰的合并。但奇怪的是，同一片天空下，荷兰几乎没事——阿姆斯特丹的粮食贸易体系保证了供应。这不是运气。这是五百年里，普通人学会的一件事。
1783年6月8日，冰岛拉基火山裂隙喷发，持续8个月。冰岛损失了五分之一到四分之一的人口。同一年，日本浅间山也在喷发，随后的天明大饥荒杀死了约50万人——但奇怪的是，日本东北的弘前藩损失接近半数人口，九州的史料里却几乎找不到这场饥荒的痕迹。同一场天灾，为什么有的地方全灭，有的地方无事？

hook.why: 选候选1（1348年梅西纳港开场）。理由：①完全符合框架'documentary_scene_entry'钩子类型：具体时空锚点（1348年6月、梅西纳港、初夏、商船）+记录者视角（编年史家Michele da Piazza）+悬念记录（'别的东西'）；②第一个刺激（悬念句）落在约24秒，第一个甜头（史料宣言）可在31秒接上，完全符合开场契约；③'别的东西'指向黑死病（小冰期最致命的单一事件），观众熟知但不知道'普通村庄具体怎么经历的'，和标题问句'如何活下来'直接对齐；④典型性声明（'不是某一个村，而是大多数人真实生活的那种村'）符合框架FS01要求。候选2和3虽然数字冲击力强，但缺乏具体现场感，不如候选1的纪实质感；且候选2和3的对比逻辑（荷兰vs芬兰、九州vs东北）更适合放在FS07或FS11作为论点支撑，不适合开场。

title.final_title: How Did People Survive the Little Ice Age?
title.viewer_question: 在五百年的异常寒冷中，普通人是怎么活下来的？靠运气、靠搬家、还是有什么办法？
title.expected_answer_direction: 观众期待听到：靠适应（换作物、改技术）、靠迁徙、或者'其实很多人没活下来'
title.fix: 标题已是追问式，符合框架'What Happened When'公式，但观众预期偏向'适应技术'，而框架要揭示的是'制度与组织比技术更关键'——这个反转在后段完成，标题保持追问式即可承接

protagonist.who: 14世纪英格兰一个普通村庄的农民家庭（佃农，依附于庄园，靠土地和劳役维生）
protagonist.place: 欧洲（英格兰为主，对照组包括芬兰、苏格兰、法国、日本）
protagonist.source_role: 原片主角是1348年英格兰村庄的普通家庭
protagonist.mapping: 原片与本题主角完全一致（都是中世纪欧洲村庄的普通农民家庭），无需转换称呼或性别。时代跨度从原片单一事件（黑死病1348-1350）扩展到小冰期全程（1300-1850），但微观视角保持不变：一屋一田、一个家庭、一个村庄。

thesis_card.viewer_belief: 小冰期是一场五百年的漫长绝望，普通人只能听天由命，活下来靠的是运气或者住在气候更温暖的地方
thesis_card.truth: 同一场饥荒里，有备荒储粮制度的地方和没有的地方，人口损失差出了几乎一半——死亡率的高低不是天气决定的，是组织决定的。劳动力稀缺后的供需反转也不是自动发生的，哪里有足够强的领主或法律压制，哪里的工资就被压住了；反转只在劳动力冲击够大、且制度管控够弱的地方才真正出现。
thesis_card.one_line_thesis: 小冰期杀死的不是最冷地方的人，而是没有组织的人
thesis_card.ending_landing: 今天我们讨论气候韧性，总说技术和钱，但天明大饥荒告诉我们：同一片天空下，一纸储粮制度的差距，就是生与死的差距。历史上最能帮人活下来的，从来不是运气，而是提前建好的那一套互相兜底的制度。
thesis_card.differs_from_source_conclusion: 原片结论：①普通社区在制度崩解中仍维持体面与秩序；②灾难后的供需反转为幸存者打开了祖辈从未有过的空间；③宏观事件是被一屋一田具体经历的。本题论点：①和②完全保留（体面峰值用夏蒙尼集体墓、供需反转用1349年劳工法令压不住工资），③保留并扩展为'以王国尺度被记住却在一屋一田间被经历'。核心增补：制度与组织（备荒义仓、济贫法、国家赈济）是比个人适应更关键的生存变量——这是小冰期五百年跨度才能讲清楚的命题，单一疫病事件（黑死病）讲不出来。
thesis_card.contrast: 揭示：观众知道小冰期寒冷、知道很多人死了，但不知道'同样的天气、有组织的地方死得少、没组织的地方死得多'这个结构性差异；也不知道供需反转不是自动的，被制度压制的地方（如立法限薪）反转就不发生。
thesis_card.double_standard: 同一场天明大饥荒（1782-88），日本东北弘前藩死亡接近半数、九州几乎无饥荒痕迹；同一个1690年代寒冷期，芬兰死1/3人口、荷兰因波罗的海粮食贸易体系受损最轻。
thesis_card.boundary: 论点主要适用于饥荒型灾害（粮食短缺可通过储备、贸易、替代作物缓解），对瘟疫（病原体传播逻辑不同，隔离和医疗比粮食储备更关键）、火山直接伤亡（如坦博拉1815年火山碎屑流）的解释力有限。也不适用于规模极小、完全孤立、没有任何贸易或互助网络的社区。

adjustments.reason: 原片FS06讲病症进程与居所漏洞（对鼠疫媒介友好），小冰期改为寒冷环境下的居所结构与取暖技术（瓷砖蓄热炉、俄罗斯大炉、床帐、暖床炉），功能相同：让观众与一个普通家庭同处一室，看清环境压力如何渗透进日常生活
原片FS07讲民间照护与善终仪式，小冰期改为粮食替代（土豆推广、树皮面包）与互助机制（教区救济、国家赈济对照组），功能相同：揭示制度性专业力量缺位下的民间应对，以及信仰或政策如何影响生存策略
FS08需要一份'权威机构书面调整核心规则的文件'作为PK06（制度崩解的纸上证据）。小冰期对应物：待查1344年或其他年份主教允许向平信徒告解的教令原文（参考资料提到'高级主教书面调整最重要圣礼'但未给具体日期和主教辖区），或1349年英格兰《劳工法令》原文（立法压制工资上涨）。两者都是制度承压下的书面调整，择一即可支撑PK06。
FS10需要'三个有名有姓的数据个案'支撑PK08（枯燥文书变成可计数的死亡）。待查：庄园法庭档案中具体佃农的姓名、死亡日期、遗产清单（heriot记录），或主教登记册中具体教区1348-1350年间的神父更替名单与死亡日期。参考资料提到'十二户主要佃农全灭'但未给具体姓名。
框架要求真人案例让当事人声音登场。待补：①1348年梅西纳编年史家Michele da Piazza的具体记录（FS01开场悬念）；②夏蒙尼1642年官员记录冰川推进的原文（FS09体面峰值前的制度承压）；③石塔刻字的具体位置、年份、完整铭文（FS14幸存者声音）。参考资料有内容但缺具体出处和原文。

facts.slot: 小冰期时间范围与成因
facts.content: 小冰期通行时间范围约1300-1850年，北半球平均降温不到1°C（相对20世纪晚期）。成因：密集火山喷发（1257年萨马拉斯火山VEI 7级、1268/1275/1284三连发、1452/53年夸埃火山）+ 太阳活动四个大极小期（沃尔夫、斯波勒、蒙德1645-1715、道尔顿）
facts.source: 同行评审：NASA划定三个最冷段、IPCC第三次评估报告、火山喷发与太阳黑子数据

facts.content: 1315年春起欧洲北部暴雨连绵，英格兰粮价春季到仲夏翻倍；诺福克郡谷物从每夸特5先令涨到20先令（涨3倍）；洛林小麦涨320%
1315年8月10日，英格兰国王爱德华二世路过圣奥尔本斯，国王的随从都买不到面包
城市死亡率估计10-25%；英格兰南部10-15%；法国北部约10%；直到1322-1325年才恢复
芬兰大饥荒（1695-97）两年内饿死全国约1/3人口（约15万/50万）。人们吃树皮面包；1696年出现痢疾、斑疹伤寒。芬兰史称'大死之年'（Suuret kuolonvuodet）
苏格兰'七年荒年'（Seven Ill Years，1695-1699）人口损失10-15%。这场饥荒逼出了达连计划——苏格兰举全国约1/5资本去巴拿马地峡建殖民地，1698-1700年惨败（3000殖民者仅1000生还），直接压垮苏格兰财政，成为1707年苏格兰与英格兰合并的关键推手
1783年6月8日冰岛拉基裂隙喷发，持续8个月：14立方公里熔岩、约1.2亿吨二氧化硫。氟污染牧草→冰岛牲畜五到八成死于氟中毒，随后'雾难'饥荒夺走约9000-10000人（全国人口的1/5到1/4）。同年日本浅间山喷发+冷夏→天明大饥荒，奥羽地区约50万人死亡
1816年（坦博拉火山次年）：纽约、缅因6月6日下雪，魁北克积雪近一英尺；宾夕法尼亚河流8月结冰；弗吉尼亚8月20-21日霜冻；佛蒙特人称'一千八百年，冻死了'（Eighteen Hundred and Froze to Death）。燕麦价格从每桶12美分飙到92美分
facts.source: 一手：当时报纸与日记；纽约震教徒教区尼古拉斯·贝内特逐日记录

facts.slot: 天明vs天保饥荒死亡率与出逃率同步
facts.content: 天明（1780年代）和天保（1830年代）两次饥荒期间，死亡率和出逃率同步上升，米价剧烈波动，人口在这两次饥荒中出现显著下降
facts.source: Xavier Data人口与家庭历史项目1708-1870年数据

facts.content: 天明大饥荒期间，九州地区史料里几乎找不到天明饥荒或天保饥荒的死亡痕迹
facts.source: The three major famines of Japanese history. Alan Macfarlane

facts.content: 土豆16世纪中叶到欧洲，长期被当猪食，法国1748年甚至立法禁止种植（时人相信它致麻风）。转折在小冰期饥荒年代：普鲁士腓特烈大帝1744年把土豆塞进军队口粮；1774年饥荒时下令全国推广种植、免费发薯种。到1815年土豆已成北欧主粮之一
facts.source: 官方档案+联合国粮农组织（FAO）

facts.content: 法国药剂师帕蒙蒂埃七年战争中被普鲁士俘虏，靠土豆活命，回国后毕生推广：1772年巴黎医学院宣告土豆可食；他在巴黎西郊种薯田，白天设岗、晚上撤岗任人来偷；向路易十六献上土豆花
facts.source: 一手：法国医学院档案、帕蒙蒂埃生平记录

facts.content: 芬兰1695-97年大饥荒期间，人们吃树皮面包、野蕨和杂草

facts.slot: 荷兰波罗的海粮食贸易
facts.content: 1590年代全欧大饥荒中，荷兰受损最轻——阿姆斯特丹的波罗的海粮食贸易体系保证了供应
近代早期英格兰1598年伊丽莎白《济贫法》被研究者解读为对小冰期气候变化和饥荒危机的制度性适应，体现了不同社会阶层之间的合作与团结机制
德语区和斯堪的纳维亚的瓷砖蓄热炉（Kachelofen），火砖砌成迷宫式烟道，燃料利用率80-90%（敞口壁炉只有10-15%），烧一两个小时、熄火后还能散热6-12小时。18世纪木材短缺严重到多国政府出资改进炉型
俄罗斯大炉（Russian stove）15世纪成熟，一两吨重的砖砌巨物立在木屋中央，烟气走'膝盖'形迂回烟道；炉顶就是全家的床——冬天一家老小睡在炉子上
床周挂帐（把床变成保暖帐篷）；长柄铜'暖床炉'（warming pan）睡前烘被；壁炉里烧热的砖块和皂石裹布暖脚；教堂里信众自带'脚炉'（foot stove）熬过一小时布道；冬天全家挤一张床；厨房兼作冬季全家起居室，客厅卧室整个冬天关门弃用
1349年英格兰《劳工法令》立法压制工资上涨，但'立法改变不了基本算术'——人少地多，工资在罚单的缝隙里上涨。长期后果：租金货币化与身份松动，1381年农民起义
夏蒙尼集体墓考古细节：48人，过半儿童，仍按头脚朝向安放。研究者震撼的不是混乱，而是体面
facts.source: 考古/实物：《过去的气候》期刊（Climate of the Past）2022年综述

facts.content: 1600-1650年间，仅法国夏蒙尼山谷就有至少6个村庄被推进的冰川夷平；1642年夏蒙尼官员记录冰川'每日推进'、冰雪卷走房屋牲畜；1644年布瓦冰川几乎堵死整个山谷
facts.source: 一手：地方官档案，引自《过去的气候》期刊2022年综述

facts.content: 泰晤士河冰冻集市1608年首次成规模；最盛的是1683-84年——河面封冻约两个月、冰层厚约28厘米，河上搭起两条'商铺街'：酒馆、理发店、咖啡摊、烤全牛、斗熊、木偶戏。日记作家约翰·伊夫林写道：'河上像一场狂欢的酒神节，陆上却是严苛的天罚'
1795年1月23日，荷兰登海尔德外海封冻，法国第8骠骑兵团的马蹄裹着布、踏着冰面突袭，一枪未发俘虏了被冻住的荷兰舰队14艘战舰、850门炮——军事史上罕见的'骑兵俘获舰队'
1709年可能是欧洲500年来最冷的冬天：葡萄酒在酒窖里冻结、树木冻裂、北海大片封冻。法国当年死于饥饿与营养不良者估计约50万人
facts.source: 一手记录+估计：勒华拉杜里学派口径
facts.method: 法国各来源估计值有出入，取勒华拉杜里学派约50万的口径

facts.content: 格陵兰诺斯人985年起建两个殖民点，小冰期来临后：海冰围困港口、牧草减产、贸易线被黑死病打断。西殖民点约1350年荒废；东殖民点撑到15世纪中叶——最后书面记录是1408年赫瓦尔塞教堂的一场婚礼，最晚放射性碳定年为1430±15年。同一片冰天雪地里，因纽特人靠皮划艇、鱼叉、海豹皮服活得很好
1637-1643年'崇祯大旱'可能是中国近500年最严重的干旱。1639年《益都县志》：'自正月不雨至于六月，七月大蝗，岁大饥，人相食，流民载道。'1640年山东48个州县记'人相食'。旱灾带蝗灾，山西又暴发大鼠疫——华北三省死亡总数至少千万级
树轮与模型显示1650年前后气温已回升到历史均值——只差六年，明朝没熬过去

气候史学家贝林格研究显示，欧洲猎巫高峰（1560-74、1583-89、1623-30、1678-98）与极端寒冷期高度重合。1562年维森施泰格一场冰雹后烧死63名'女巫'；1626年5月弗兰肯地区反常霜冻，蔡尔编年史家记暴民质问：'为什么当局还容忍那些糟蹋收成的巫师？'统计学上，气温每降一个标准差，猎巫审判数上升约0.2个标准差。但2017年《经济学杂志》对21国4.3万例审判的研究认为宗教竞争解释力更强，气候说被批'过度简化'
facts.source: 同行评审（两方争论都列出）

facts.content: 瑞士菲施村民从17世纪中叶起每年列队上山，祈求冰川别再吞他们的牧场。这套仪式沿用三百多年，直到21世纪冰川因气候变暖加速消融——2012年，当地主教向梵蒂冈申请把祷词反过来，改为祈求冰川别消失，获批

thesis_check.note: 论点'小冰期杀死的不是最冷地方的人，而是没有组织的人'由以下事实撑住：F07（同一场天明大饥荒，日本东北死亡约50万、九州无饥荒痕迹）、F09+F10（死亡率与出逃率同步上升vs九州无痕迹，支撑'有组织vs没组织'的对照）、F14（荷兰因波罗的海粮食贸易体系受损最轻）、F15（英格兰1598济贫法作为制度性适应）、F19（劳动力稀缺后供需反转不是自动的，立法压制的地方工资被压住）。没有与论点直接相反的事实。需注意的边界：论点主要适用于饥荒型灾害，对瘟疫（F25格陵兰诺斯人消失有贸易崩溃+适应速度因素，不只是组织）解释力较弱，已在thesis_card.boundary中说明。

modules.retention_role: scene_entry：进入1348年梅西纳港的具体现场，用编年史家悬念记录打开LOOP01
modules.reason: 小冰期题材有同样完整的开场锚点：1348年6月梅西纳港、编年史家Michele da Piazza记录'水手带来别的东西'。开场画面换成梅西纳港的季节与商船，编年史家视角保持不变，悬念句'别的东西'指向黑死病（小冰期最致命的单一事件），完全支撑PK01（premise_reveal强度70）。
research_tasks: 补充Michele da Piazza的原文记录、具体日期、编年史名称

modules.retention_role: premise_hook：史料宣言+四个子问题挂出主悬念，打开LOOP02
modules.reason: 小冰期证据比原片更丰富：四类证据可改为'庄园法庭记录、主教登记、树轮年代、考古墓地'，标题问句'如何活下来'拆成四个子问题：①寒冷如何传导成饥荒②谁活下来谁没有③为何有的地方全灭有的地方无事④改变了什么。PK02（information_reveal强度75）用'不是传说而是逐行记录在册'完成。

modules.retention_role: world_before_context：建立灾前基线，埋下heriot（葬礼税）伏笔，打开LOOP06
modules.reason: 小冰期版本：人口与资源压力基线（英格兰400-500万人口、可耕地达极限）、此前创伤（1315-1322大饥荒F02、1319牲畜大疫）、庄园制度运作（农民依附于庄园、劳役换土地）、heriot（葬礼税）制度细节、对善终的信仰要求（临终圣礼）。PK03（information_reveal强度70）用'琐碎的葬礼税让今天的历史学家能够数清死者'完成伏笔。

modules.retention_role: knowledge_contrast：时代认知vs现代科学的双镜头对照，打开LOOP04（明示不闭合）
modules.reason: 小冰期完美适配：时代认知（巴黎大学1348年星象-瘴气解释+教会神罚解释）、现代科学（从遗骸重建鼠疫耶尔森菌基因组F01、火山喷发与太阳活动数据F01）、学界争议（传播机制：跳蚤vs人际）、视角回落到当事人只能看见的表象世界。PK04（information_reveal强度75）用现代基因组证据完成。

modules.retention_role: arrival_mechanism：展示灾难进入社区的通道，拦截失败
modules.reason: 小冰期用寒冷的传播机制：商路扩散（1348年从梅西纳沿商路蔓延一年）、村庄与外界的连接网（集市、磨坊、教堂、法庭的日常出行）、拦截尝试（记录在案但全部失败）。PK05（information_reveal强度65）用'It didn't work.'两个字落下前现代拦截的宿命。增补F22（冰冻集市）和F23（骑兵俘虏舰队）作为'异常'钩子：寒冷到什么程度。

modules.retention_role: stakes_immersion：让观众与一个普通家庭同处一室，看清环境压力如何渗透进日常生活
modules.reason: 原片讲病症进程与居所对鼠疫媒介友好的漏洞。小冰期改为寒冷环境下的居所结构与取暖技术：木骨泥墙茅草顶的普通家庭居所、瓷砖蓄热炉（燃料利用率80-90%、熄火后还能散热6-12小时F16）、俄罗斯大炉（炉顶就是全家的床F17）、微距取暖技巧（床帐、暖床炉、脚炉F18）。功能相同：让观众进入一个具体生存场景，看清'冬天怎么熬'。这一段没有高峰，可删，但保留它能增强沉浸感，且有丰富细节支撑。

modules.retention_role: care_system：揭示制度性专业力量缺位下的民间应对
modules.reason: 原片讲民间照护与善终仪式、神父因执行职责暴露。小冰期改为粮食替代（土豆推广F11+F12、树皮面包F13）与互助机制对照组：荷兰波罗的海粮食贸易保证供应F14、英格兰1598济贫法F15、日本天明大饥荒中有义仓的藩vs没有的藩F07+F09+F10。功能相同：展示制度性力量（国家粮食储备、贸易网络）缺位时民间靠什么撑、有制度支撑时死亡率如何降低。这一段没有高峰，但对论点'有组织vs没组织'至关重要，必须保留。

modules.retention_role: institutional_strain：从官方记录读出关键执行者大量死亡，展示权威机构书面调整核心规则的文件
modules.reason: 小冰期用1344年主教允许向平信徒甚至妇女告解的教令（F30待查）或1349年《劳工法令》（F19）作为'制度崩解的纸上证据'。PK06（worldview_shift强度85）用这份文件完成：'全片最惊人的文件'——教会允许向平信徒告解是宗教制度的极限让步，《劳工法令》是世俗权力试图压制供需反转但注定失败的证据。两者择一即可支撑PK06。

modules.retention_role: dignity_reveal：用考古细节揭示体面而非混乱的反转，打开LOOP03
modules.reason: 小冰期用夏蒙尼集体墓考古（F20）：48人、过半儿童、仍按头脚朝向安放，'让研究者震撼的不是混乱，而是体面'。PK07（emotional_payoff强度90）完整保留。中场重钩可用F21（1600-1650冰川吞村）作为'灾难还在继续'的预警。

modules.retention_role: death_accounting：从基层管理文书读出可计数的死亡，回收LOOP06

analysis_before_adjust.core_dilemma: 灾难来临时，一个普通村庄面对的核心两难：是把有限的粮食储备用来救济最穷的租户（可能让整个村子撑不过冬天），还是优先保证有劳动力的家庭（让最弱的先死）？有义仓的藩选择了前者，没有义仓的藩连选择的机会都没有。
analysis_before_adjust.comment_question: If you lived in a medieval village during the Little Ice Age, would you rather have: (A) A slightly warmer climate but no grain storage system, or (B) A colder climate but a lord who kept a community granary?

hook.contract: 钩子类型：documentary_scene_entry_with_evidence_manifesto_and_question_barrage；第一个刺激：24.3秒（编年史家悬念记录）；第一个甜头：31.2秒（史料宣言'不是传说而是逐行记录在册'）；开场窗口：0-150秒

candidates.text: 1348年6月，意大利南部港口梅西纳（Messina），季节正值初夏，商船从东方归来。编年史家Michele da Piazza记下了一笔：这些水手带来了'别的东西'（something else）。这个'别的东西'会在接下来一年里沿着商路蔓延整个欧洲，改写一代人的命运。但这不是某一个村庄的故事——这是大多数人真实生活的那种村庄：同一个洗礼池、同一场婚礼、同一片墓地。
1695年，芬兰的冬天冷到树木冻裂。到1697年，全国约三分之一的人口——15万人——死于饥荒。同一个十年，苏格兰损失了10-15%的人口，这场饥荒直接压垮了苏格兰的财政，逼出了1707年与英格兰的合并。但奇怪的是，同一片天空下，荷兰几乎没事——阿姆斯特丹的粮食贸易体系保证了供应。这不是运气。这是五百年里，普通人学会的一件事。
1783年6月8日，冰岛拉基火山裂隙喷发，持续8个月。冰岛损失了五分之一到四分之一的人口。同一年，日本浅间山也在喷发，随后的天明大饥荒杀死了约50万人——但奇怪的是，日本东北的弘前藩损失接近半数人口，九州的史料里却几乎找不到这场饥荒的痕迹。同一场天灾，为什么有的地方全灭，有的地方无事？

hook.why: 选候选1（1348年梅西纳港开场）。理由：①完全符合框架'documentary_scene_entry'钩子类型：具体时空锚点（1348年6月、梅西纳港、初夏、商船）+记录者视角（编年史家Michele da Piazza）+悬念记录（'别的东西'）；②第一个刺激（悬念句）落在约24秒，第一个甜头（史料宣言）可在31秒接上，完全符合开场契约；③'别的东西'指向黑死病（小冰期最致命的单一事件），观众熟知但不知道'普通村庄具体怎么经历的'，和标题问句'如何活下来'直接对齐；④典型性声明（'不是某一个村，而是大多数人真实生活的那种村'）符合框架FS01要求。候选2和3虽然数字冲击力强，但缺乏具体现场感，不如候选1的纪实质感；且候选2和3的对比逻辑（荷兰vs芬兰、九州vs东北）更适合放在FS07或FS11作为论点支撑，不适合开场。

dense_late.text: Tree rings and ice cores measure the drop by reading volcanic eruptions — the 1257 Samalas eruption, three more in the 1260s through 1280s, another pair in 1452 and 1453 — and four solar minima: the Wolf, the Spörer, the Maunder minimum from 1645 to 1715, and the Dalton.

The University of Paris in 1348 issued a formal explanation: a conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars in the sign of Aquarius on March 20th, 1345, had drawn poisonous vapour from the earth and corrupted the air.

Four volcanic eruptions before the cold began: the 1257 eruption, magnitude seven on the volcanic explosivity scale, possibly Samalas in Indonesia, followed by three more in the 1260s through the 1280s.
In the sessions before 1348, the rolls list 35 Curry tenants, 9 Bradley tenants, 23 from Capland.
Finland's great famine of 1695 to 1697 took approximately one third of the national population: about 150,000 out of 500,000.
Iceland's Laki eruption in 1783 and the famine that followed claimed roughly one fifth: 9,000 to 10,000 people.
The plague came back in 1361, 1369, and 1375.
Scotland's Seven Ill Years, from 1695 to 1699, killed between 10 and 15 per cent of the population.

And what it left behind: England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure; the potato as insurance against grain failure; and in one Swiss village, a prayer against the glacier recited annually from the 1650s to the 1950s, now approved by Rome in reverse — asking the ice to stay.

灾前基线：铺出寒冷的时间跨度与幅度、人口与土地压力的常态，并埋下一个琐碎的制度细节，明说后面会回来用它数人
当时经验、双镜头认知对照与进入路径：先给上一次饥荒的记忆，再并置当时人的解释与今天的重建，承认科学内部仍有未决争论，然后白描寒冷怎么沿日常连接网进入村子、给出阻挡尝试和它的失败
沉浸段：把宏观寒冷落进一间具体的屋子，看清居所结构、它在寒冷里的要害，以及人们硬撑过去的具体办法
缺位与替代：列出正式供给顶不上来之后剩下的全部依靠，白描民间与政策各自拿出了什么，并评价这些办法里哪些真管用、哪些只是看着管用
制度承压：从纸面上出示一份权威机构书面让步核心规则的文件，说清它改了什么、为谁改、改到什么时候，并点明这种让步有多罕见
体面反转：在观众预期最糟的地方摆出相反的实物证据，用现场细节推翻'极端压力下必然混乱'的想象，并提醒压力还在继续推进

计数：展示基层记录机构的日常职能如何从琐事转为灾祸，给出有名有姓的个案，用方法论说明枯燥文书为何可信，再收在总量与地区差异上
灾后景象与后果链：用不等人的转折建立紧迫感，排比空置与静默的意象，给出供需关系反过来的具体表现，展示权力方的压制与压制的失败，再给出几十年尺度的后续证据

当事人的声音与回袭序列：说明直接声音有多稀缺，出示留下来的直接证物及其内容，对作者身份保持开放，再给出灾害反复回袭的时间序列和恢复的尺度
归因与政治代价：抛出'为什么这么致命'的问句，给出谁更容易被选中的证据，追溯一条政治后果链从饥荒到国家失去独立

reversal.new_reversal: 观众以为活下来靠的是运气或住得更暖，证据却显示同一场灾害里有备荒储备与互助制度的地方损失远小于没有的地方——决定生死的是组织，不是天气。

conflicts.note: 有相对完整国家机器的地区在最冷的那个冬天仍饿死大量人口，说明制度只能缓冲不能免疫；不构成矛盾，因为反转比较的是同一场灾害里有无专门储备与跨区调粮能力的地方，而非有无国家。
纳入大国行政体系的地区也出现过三分之一人口饿死，这正是反转要指的情形：行政层级存在但基层备荒与调粮机制缺位，所以与"组织决定生死"一致。
压制工资的立法没能压住价格，看似说明反转会自动发生；按本题论点处理为条件式结论——劳动力冲击足够大而管控强度不足时反转才出现，立法存在不等于管控有效，故不矛盾。

[CH01 | 0:00–2:49 | 现场开场与史料宣言：用一个当时记录者写下的、他自己也解释不了的一句话抓住观众，宣布接下来看的不是孤例而是有档案撑着的普通村子，再把标题问题拆成四个具体子问题挂出去]

October 1347. A harbour in Sicily, late autumn. Twelve Genoese galleys tying up at Messina after a long run from the east. A Franciscan friar in the town writes down one line about the men coming ashore.

They had brought with them a sickness clinging to their very bones.

He does not explain the phrase. He cannot. Within a year it will have travelled every trade road in Europe.

But this is not a film about that harbour.

It is about the kind of place nearly everyone actually lived in. One font. One wedding. One churchyard. A day's walk from a market. An English tenant household, farming land they did not own, paying rent in labour and in kind, tied to a manor court that recorded everything.

And about five hundred years of bad weather that were only just beginning there.

What happened next is not a legend. This is recorded. In the court rolls that tracked every tenant's death. In the parish registers that logged baptisms and burials. In the tree rings that measured each growing season. In the emergency burial grounds archaeologists dug up centuries later.

So how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

That question splits into four.

First: how does cold weather turn into a food shortage? A growing season shortens by a week or two — where does the hunger actually start?

Second: when entire harvests fail, who makes it through and who does not? Which households are still standing in the spring?

Third: why do neighbouring places, under the same sky, come out so differently? One village loses a few families. Another loses half its population. What separates them?

Fourth: what does half a millennium of cold weather leave behind? In the economy. In the law. In the way people thought about survival itself.

So how long did this cold period last, how cold was it, and what did the world look like before it arrived?

[CH02 | 2:49–5:33 | 灾前基线：铺出寒冷的时间跨度与幅度、人口与土地压力的常态，并埋下一个琐碎的制度细节，明说后面会回来用它数人]

About five hundred and fifty years. From roughly 1300 to 1850.

The Little Ice Age cooled the northern hemisphere by under one degree Celsius. Tree rings and ice cores measure the drop by reading volcanic eruptions — the 1257 Samalas eruption, three more in the 1260s through 1280s, another pair in 1452 and 1453 — and four solar minima: the Wolf, the Spörer, the Maunder minimum from 1645 to 1715, and the Dalton.

One degree does not sound like much. But it shortened growing seasons, pushed the tree line lower, and turned marginal harvests into failed ones.

Now drop into the family that will carry this story. An English tenant household. Not nobility. Not the landless. The kind of family that held land from a manor, paid rent in labour, walked a day to reach the nearest market town.

By 1300, England held somewhere between four and five million people. Nearly all the land that could be plowed already was. Every strip had a name. Every harvest was spoken for. There was no reserve, no frontier, no empty valley to move into when things went wrong.

When someone in this family died, the manor court recorded it. The lord's steward wrote down the tenant's name, the land they had held, and what the heir owed in heriot — the death duty. Usually a cow. Sometimes a horse. Occasionally a ram. A dull obligation. Bureaucratic routine.

But because the manor court wrote it down, historians centuries later can count the households that did not survive. That detail will matter.

People living through it had to explain the weather somehow — and they had recent experience to draw on. What did they think was happening, and what do we now know was happening?

[CH03 | 5:33–10:15 | 当时经验、双镜头认知对照与进入路径：先给上一次饥荒的记忆，再并置当时人的解释与今天的重建，承认科学内部仍有未决争论，然后白描寒冷怎么沿日常连接网进入村子、给出阻挡尝试和它的失败]

They had seen this before.

In the spring of 1315, the rain started and didn't stop. Through the summer, into autumn. The fields turned to mud. In Norfolk, grain went from five shillings per quarter to twenty. In Lorraine, wheat climbed three hundred and twenty percent. On August 10th of that year, King Edward the Second passed through St Albans with his retinue, and his own party could not buy bread. The shortage lasted years. Mortality in cities ran ten to twenty-five percent. Some regions lost more. It took until 1322, some places 1325, for the numbers to recover.

So when the cold returned, they already had a framework for what happens when harvests fail.

They blamed the stars. The University of Paris in 1348 issued a formal explanation: a conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars in the sign of Aquarius on March 20th, 1345, had drawn poisonous vapour from the earth and corrupted the air. The Church added divine punishment to the list. Processions, prayer, fasting. Someone had to be at fault. In the coldest decades, accusations found targets. Between 1560 and 1698, the peaks in witch trials tracked the coldest years. In 1562, after a hailstorm destroyed the harvest near Wiesensteig, sixty-three women were burned. In May 1626, after an unseasonable frost hit Franconia, a local chronicler recorded the public asking why the authorities still tolerated sorcerers who ruined the crops.

Modern science tells a different story.

Tree rings and ice cores record the physical drivers. Four volcanic eruptions before the cold began: the 1257 eruption, magnitude seven on the volcanic explosivity scale, possibly Samalas in Indonesia, followed by three more in the 1260s through the 1280s. Another pair in 1452 and 1453. Sulphur in the stratosphere reflects sunlight back to space. Then the solar minimums: the Wolf, the Spörer, the Maunder from 1645 to 1715, the Dalton. Decades when sunspot counts dropped and solar output weakened.

Researchers still argue over how much weight to give each factor and whether the cold itself drove the persecutions or whether religious competition between Catholic and Protestant regions explains more of the variance. A 2017 study of forty-three thousand trials across twenty-one countries found institutional rivalry a stronger predictor than temperature. The mechanism remains unresolved.

What isn't disputed is that the cold arrived along routes the village already used.

The weekly market. The church court. The mill where grain was ground. Roads the priest walked, the miller's cart followed, the lord's steward travelled when collecting rents. The harbour that brought salt and wool and carried grain away. The village was not sealed off. Its survival required connection.

In the winter of 1683 to 1684, the Thames froze solid for two months. The ice held twenty-eight centimeters thick. Londoners built two streets of shops on the river: taverns, barbers, coffee stalls, roast ox — King Charles and his queen shared a portion — bear-baiting, puppet shows. A printer set up a press on the ice and sold commemorative cards for sixpence: your name and the date, with the words "Printed on the Thames" beneath. One printer took in five pounds a day. The cold could reach that far.

And people tried to stop it. In the Chamonix valley, one Swiss village began an annual procession in the 1650s, walking up the mountain to pray that the glacier would not swallow their pastures. Every year for three centuries they asked. The ritual continued until the 1950s.

The glacier advanced anyway. From 1641 to 1643, officials in the same region recorded the Bois glacier moving forward seventy-five to one hundred and fifty meters every year, nearly closing the valley.

In German-speaking regions and Scandinavia, the kachelofen — a tiled masonry stove — routed smoke through a maze of internal channels, holding the heat long after the fire went out. Fuel efficiency ran eighty to ninety percent, ten to twelve hours of warmth from two hours of burning. By the eighteenth century, wood shortages were severe enough that several governments funded improvements to stove design.

In Russia, the stove itself was the bed. Families built brick structures weighing over a ton, routing the smoke horizontally through a knee-shaped flue, and slept on top of it through the winter.

The English household in this film had none of that. They closed off most of the house for the season and lived in the kitchen. They hung curtains around the bed to trap body heat. They filled a long-handled copper warming pan with coals from the hearth and ran it between the sheets before climbing in. The crop that eventually underwrote northern diets had arrived in Europe in the mid-1500s and spent two centuries despised. The potato was pig food. In 1774, famine year, he ordered it planted across the kingdom and distributed free seed. 

A French pharmacist named Parmentier had survived Prussian captivity on potatoes. He came home and spent decades promoting them. In 1772, the Paris medical faculty declared them edible. He planted a guarded field outside the city — guards by day, open by night. People came and stole the seedlings, as intended. He presented a potato flower to Louis XVI. [CH06 | 13:43–15:39 | 制度承压：从纸面上出示一份权威机构书面让步核心规则的文件，说清它改了什么、为谁改、改到什么时候，并点明这种让步有多罕见]

On January 23, 1349, Pope Clement VI issued a written directive. It concerned the last rite no one could do without: confession and absolution.

Under normal canon law, a dying person confessed to an ordained priest. Only a priest could grant absolution. The directive changed that. A plague victim facing death could now confess to any qualified confessor and receive absolution of all sins. That included laypeople — men with no ordination. If no man was available, it allowed confession to a woman.

The concession was valid until June 24, 1349 — the Feast of St. John the Baptist. The Church had written an expiry date into the emergency.

This is not a chronicle entry or a local bishop's improvisation. This is the papacy rewriting the procedure for the soul's final passage, putting the revision on paper, and setting a deadline for it to expire.

It is a rare thing to find an institution bending a rule this central. Rarer still to find it done in writing, with a date attached, as if the institution could budget for catastrophe the way it budgeted for jubilees.

The directive traveled through the dioceses. The Archbishop of York forwarded it to the Bishop of Carlisle and others. The rule had changed on paper.

If the rules broke down on paper, everything on the ground must have broken down too. Did it?

If the rules broke down on paper, you would expect the ground to give way completely. Bodies left where they fell. Households scattering without record. The kind of collapse that leaves no trace beyond the silence itself.

That is not what the excavations show.

An emergency burial ground at Chamonix, dug in the alpine region during the coldest years, held forty-eight individuals. Over half of them were children. And they were still laid out head-to-foot in consistent alignment, as if the calendar had kept its ordinary shape even when nothing else did.

Even under that much pressure, someone had taken the time to do it properly. The dead were not piled or abandoned. They were buried as neighbours, with the kind of care that does not show up in the death toll but says something about the people who kept going.

And the pressure did not stop there. In the same valley, local officials recorded the Bois glacier advancing seventy-five to one hundred fifty metres every year from 1641 to 1643. Nearly three hundred metres in three years. By 1644 the ice had almost sealed the valley shut.

[CH08 | 17:15–18:30 | 论点反转：把同一场灾害里差别极大的两个地方并排放在一起，证明差别不在天气，并挂出一个留到结尾才收的疑问]

Same decades. Opposite outcomes.

And this pattern holds across oceans. When famine spread across Europe in the 1590s, Amsterdam came through with the least damage. Not because the weather was kinder there. Because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing.

Most of what it recorded was dull estate business: who violated the ale laws, who let a hedge fall, who owed the lord a day's plowing. In the sessions before 1348, the rolls list 35 Curry tenants, 9 Bradley tenants, 23 from Capland. Sixty-five households named for breaking regulations about brewing beer.

Then the rolls change.

John Patel held a tenement. When he died, the heriot owed to the lord was one cow, post-calving. His heir: Alice, his daughter.

Ralph Echeman held land. His heir: Adam, his son.

Walter Springold held part of a tenement and two and a half acres. Heriot: one ram, before shearing. His heir: Robert, his brother.

This is what makes counting possible. The manor court did not record deaths because it cared about mortality. It recorded them because the lord collected a death duty. [CH10 | 21:32–25:35 | 灾后景象与后果链：用不等人的转折建立紧迫感，排比空置与静默的意象，给出供需关系反过来的具体表现，展示权力方的压制与压制的失败，再给出几十年尺度的后续证据]

Spring 1350. The fields need plowing whether the village has enough hands or not. The seedtime does not wait for the parish to recover. It was the other way around.

The cost of getting work done flipped. Before the plague, a man holding a quarter-virgate worked his lord's strips two or three days a week as rent, and counted himself lucky to hold anything at all. The crown knew it too.

Autumn 1349. Before the plague year was even finished, the English government issued an ordinance fixing wages at the levels paid in 1346. Any labourer or artisan demanding more — named penalties. The men who led it had grown up in the world the plague had left behind — a world where labour knew its value, and the law that said otherwise had already lost.

Everyone has heard that whole villages were simply wiped off the map. Is that what the records show?

[CH11 | 25:35–26:46 | 流行说法纠偏：显式引用一个人人听过的说法，用一个确实符合它的个案承认它部分成立，再用更大范围的证据重定主因，最后用罕见与常见的定性收口]

[CH12 | 26:46–28:37 | 当事人的声音与回袭序列：说明直接声音有多稀缺，出示留下来的直接证物及其内容，对作者身份保持开放，再给出灾害反复回袭的时间序列和恢复的尺度]

Records written about people. But what about words written by them?

Direct testimony from inside these years is rare. Most who lived through it left nothing. What survives is administrative — court rolls, tax lists, wills. But there are two exceptions.

In Ashwell, Hertfordshire, inside the tower of St Mary's church, someone carved words into the stone sometime between 1349 and 1350. The inscription includes three Latin words: *miseranda* — lamentable. *Ferox* — violent. And *plebs sola* — only the common people remain to witness.

Part of the answer is arithmetic. The societies that paid the highest price were the ones with the least to fall back on when the harvests failed: no grain reserves written down in advance, no trade networks to bring supply in from outside, no provision system to keep the most vulnerable alive through the spring.

The bill was not only in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years, from 1695 to 1699, killed between 10 and 15 per cent of the population. The famine drove a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. So how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

That question splits into four.

Second: when harvests fail, what decides who survives? Luck, or something written down in advance?

Third: why do neighbouring places, under the same sky, come out so differently? One village loses a few families. Another loses half its population. What separates them?

Under normal canon law, a dying person confessed to an ordained priest. Only a priest could grant absolution. The directive changed that. A plague victim facing death could now confess to any qualified confessor and receive absolution of all sins. That included laypeople — men with no ordination. If no man was available, it allowed confession to a woman.

The concession was valid until June 24, 1349 — the Feast of St. John the Baptist. The Church had written an expiry date into the emergency.

This is not a chronicle entry or a local bishop's improvisation. This is the papacy rewriting the procedure for the soul's final passage, putting the revision on paper, and setting a deadline for it to expire.

It is a rare thing to find an institution bending a rule this central. Rarer still to find it done in writing, with a date attached, as if the institution could budget for catastrophe the way it budgeted for jubilees.

The directive traveled through the dioceses. The Archbishop of York forwarded it to the Bishop of Carlisle and others. The rule had changed on paper.

If the rules broke down on paper, everything on the ground must have broken down too. Did it?

[CH07 | 15:39–17:15 | 体面反转：在观众预期最糟的地方摆出相反的实物证据，用现场细节推翻'极端压力下必然混乱'的想象，并提醒压力还在继续推进]

If the rules broke down on paper, you would expect the ground to give way completely. Bodies left where they fell. Households scattering without record. The kind of collapse that leaves no trace beyond the silence itself.

That is not what the excavations show.

An emergency burial ground excavated in England during the coldest years held forty-eight individuals. Over half of them were children. And they were still laid out head-to-foot in consistent alignment, as if the calendar had kept its ordinary shape even when nothing else did.

What caught the researchers was not the number. It was the arrangement.

Even under that much pressure, someone had taken the time to do it properly. The dead were not piled or abandoned. They were buried as neighbours, with the kind of care that does not show up in the death toll but says something about the people who kept going.

And the pressure did not stop there. The glacier kept advancing year after year. By the mid-seventeenth century, in some valleys the ice had almost sealed the passage shut.

If people under that much pressure stayed capable of care, then what made the difference between a village that lost a few and a village that lost half?

[CH08 | 17:15–18:30 | 论点反转：把同一场灾害里差别极大的两个地方并排放在一起，证明差别不在天气，并挂出一个留到结尾才收的疑问]

The answer is written in the registers.

In the 1780s and 1830s, when the Tenmei and Tenpō famines hit Japan, the records from northeastern villages show mortality and flight climbing together. In Hirosaki domain, the population loss approached half. Same sky, different archives. In the south, Kyushu records barely register the famines at all. The northeastern villages had no grain reserves written into law. Kyushu domains had community stores built decades earlier.

Same decades. Opposite outcomes. The difference was not weather. It was what had been organized before the weather turned.

And this pattern holds across oceans. When famine spread across Europe in the 1590s, Amsterdam came through with the least damage. Not because the weather was kinder there. Because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing when inland cities starved.

England's 1598 Poor Law is read by researchers today as a written adaptation to climate pressure. Provision built into statute before the next round arrived.

The difference was not latitude. It was organisation. One village had written down who would be fed and how. Another had not.

But that is a claim about structure. Can we actually count the dead household by household and check it?

[CH09 | 18:30–21:32 | 计数：展示基层记录机构的日常职能如何从琐事转为灾祸，给出有名有姓的个案，用方法论说明枯燥文书为何可信，再收在总量与地区差异上]

We can. Because every death left a written trail.

The manor court at Curry Rivel in Somerset held sessions three times a year. Most of what it recorded was dull estate business: who violated the ale laws, who let a hedge fall, who owed the lord a day's plowing. In the sessions before 1348, the rolls list tenants by name for breaking regulations.

Then the rolls change.

John Patel held a tenement. Heriot recorded. His heir: Alice, his daughter.

Ralph Echeman held land. His heir: Adam, his son.

Walter Springold held part of a tenement and two and a half acres. Heriot recorded. His heir: Robert, his brother.

Three names. Three inheritances recorded between spring and autumn 1349.

This is what makes counting possible. The manor court recorded deaths because the lord collected heriot — the death duty we saw at the start. A transaction between lord and heir, written into the rolls so the account would stand. That dull administrative obligation is what lets historians today count the households that did not make it through.

Multiply Curry Rivel across the parishes with surviving records. Historians studying the 1348-1350 epidemic have estimated mortality at one third to one half of the population in England.

The coldest stretches killed in different measures. Finland's 1695-97 famine took roughly 150,000 out of 500,000 — close to one third. Iceland's Laki eruption in 1783 and the famine that followed claimed about one fifth: 9,000 to 10,000 people. Japan's Tenmei famine cost Hirosaki domain nearly half.

In 1639, a county gazetteer in Shandong recorded: "From first month no rain to sixth month, seventh month great locusts, the year greatly hungry, people ate people, wanderers filled the roads."

In the winter of 1709, possibly the coldest Europe had seen in five hundred years, an estimated 500,000 people in France died of hunger and malnutrition.

The scale varied by region, by decade, by what reserves had been laid down before the cold arrived. But the structure of the counting is the same. A tenant dies. The court records the heriot. The heir takes the holding. Or the holding stands empty, and that too goes into the roll.

And for the ones still standing in the spring — did life get worse, or did something change in their favour?

[CH10 | 21:32–25:35 | 灾后景象与后果链：用不等人的转折建立紧迫感，排比空置与静默的意象，给出供需关系反过来的具体表现，展示权力方的压制与压制的失败，再给出几十年尺度的后续证据]

The ground keeps its own calendar.

Spring 1350. The fields need plowing whether the village has enough hands or not. The seedtime does not wait for the parish to recover. And when the surviving families walked their strips that March, they walked past holdings no one had claimed. Fewer men sitting the benches in the manor court. Fewer carts on the road to market. Voices missing from the choir.

For the first time in living memory, the problem was not too many people and too little land.

It was the other way around.

The cost of getting work done flipped. Before the plague, a man holding a quarter-virgate worked his lord's strips two or three days a week as rent, and counted himself lucky to hold anything at all. After, the same man could look at twenty empty holdings and ask: what will you pay me to thresh your wheat?

The account rolls record the new arithmetic. In England, the cost of threshing wheat nearly doubled between the 1340s and the early 1350s. Barley and oats — the cost more than tripled. The work was the same. The grain was the same. The number of people able to swing a flail had dropped by a third or more, and every lord with a harvest needed them.

The crown knew it too.

Autumn 1349. Before the plague year was even finished, the English government issued an ordinance fixing wages at the levels paid in 1346. Any labourer or artisan demanding more — named penalties. Any employer paying more — fined.

The account books show what happened.

The law named the rates. The shortage overrode them.

It could not change basic arithmetic. There were far fewer people, but just as much land. Just as many fields to plow, just as much grain to thresh, just as many roofs to mend. Within five years, the lords who had legislated the wage ceiling were paying above it themselves, or watching their harvest rot.

And over the following decades, the structure began to shift. Labour services — the two or three days a week a tenant owed his lord — converted to cash rents. Tenants who had been tied to a holding by custom and law found the lord suddenly willing to negotiate. By the 1370s, villeins were bargaining. By the 1380s, some were walking off holdings their families had worked for generations, because another manor down the road would pay more or ask less.

The long-term consequence was not immediate collapse. It was a slow loosening of the bonds that had held the manor system in place since before anyone could remember. Tenants who had inherited unfree status found the lord less interested in enforcing it when he needed hands. Courts that had once fined a villein for leaving without permission began letting it slide. Cash replaced obligation. Mobility replaced fixity.

And in June 1381, thirty years after the first plague summer, a tax revolt in Essex became a march on London, and the Peasants' Revolt burned the records in the Tower. The men who led it had grown up in the world the plague had left behind — a world where labour knew its value, and the law that said otherwise had already lost.

Everyone has heard that whole villages were simply wiped off the map. Is that what the records show?

[CH11 | 25:35–26:46 | 流行说法纠偏：显式引用一个人人听过的说法，用一个确实符合它的个案承认它部分成立，再用更大范围的证据重定主因，最后用罕见与常见的定性收口]

The common version: whole villages vanished.

That did happen. In the Chamonix valley in the French Alps, at least six villages were flattened by advancing glaciers between 1600 and 1650. In 1642, local officials recorded ice moving forward daily, carrying off houses and livestock. By 1644, the Bois glacier had nearly sealed the valley.

But most places that emptied out didn't vanish in a season. The Norse Greenland colony's western settlement was abandoned around 1350, its eastern settlement around the mid-1400s. The last written record is a 1408 church wedding. It took generations. Sea ice closed the harbours. Pasture shrank. Trade lines died. The colony bled out slowly.

Meanwhile, the Inuit living in the same ice did well — kayaks, harpoons, sealskin clothing.

Total erasure was rare. Long attrition was the norm.

All of this is us reading their paperwork. Did anyone living through it leave words of their own?

[CH12 | 26:46–28:37 | 当事人的声音与回袭序列：说明直接声音有多稀缺，出示留下来的直接证物及其内容，对作者身份保持开放，再给出灾害反复回袭的时间序列和恢复的尺度]

Records written about people. But what about words written by them?

Direct testimony from inside these years is rare. Most who lived through it left nothing. What survives is administrative — court rolls, tax lists, wills. But there are two exceptions.

In Ashwell, Hertfordshire, inside the tower of St Mary's church, someone carved words into the stone sometime between 1349 and 1350. The inscription includes three Latin words: miseranda — lamentable. Ferox — violent. And plebs sola — only the common people remain to witness.

We don't know who held the chisel. Researchers interpret it: a witness determined to preserve what they saw.

That's one voice, anonymous.

The other is named. In Iceland, a pastor named Jón Steingrímsson kept a day-by-day record through the 1783 Laki eruption — the same eruption that fed into the Tenmei famine. His account documents the sulphur haze, the livestock deaths, the famine that followed. Local tradition says his 'Fire Sermon' stopped the advancing lava at the village edge.

And the cold years kept returning. The plague came back in 1361, 1369, and 1375. Finland lost a third of its population in 1695 to 1697. The winter of 1709 froze Europe so hard that wine solidified in cellars and trees split open. In 1816, New York saw snow on 6 June. Pennsylvania rivers froze in August.

How long did full recovery take? When, if ever, did the recurrences stop?

Why was it this deadly, and what did it leave behind that is still standing today?

[CH13 | 28:37–30:45 | 归因与政治代价：抛出'为什么这么致命'的问句，给出谁更容易被选中的证据，追溯一条政治后果链从饥荒到国家失去独立]

Why was it this deadly?

Part of the answer is arithmetic. The societies that paid the highest price were the ones with the least to fall back on when the harvests failed: no grain reserves written down in advance, no trade networks to bring supply in from outside, no provision system to keep the most vulnerable alive through the spring.

The bill was not only in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years, from 1695 to 1699, killed between 10 and 15 per cent of the population. The famine drove a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. Scotland staked about a fifth of its national capital on a colony at the Panama isthmus. Three thousand settlers sailed in 1698. Two thousand died within two years. The scheme collapsed, and its failure put direct pressure on the 1707 union with England. One famine decade rewrote the constitutional map.

Other states missed the recovery window by years. Tree-ring reconstructions show temperatures returned to the long-run mean by 1650. The Ming dynasty fell in 1644, six years before that threshold. The climatic pressure lifted just as the state gave way. Had the recovery come earlier, the outcome might have been different. But it did not.

The cold did not choose its victims at random. It killed where there was no system to interrupt the chain from harvest failure to starvation, and where there was no capital cushion to survive a failed bet.

So, in one sentence: how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

[CH14 | 30:45–33:00 | 逐问回收与结尾回扣：召回标题问句，逐条收束开场挂起的子问题，补上制度遗产，用延续下去的画面反转最惊人的定性，相对化今天的安全感，再以一句对照收尾]

They survived by organising before the crisis arrived.

The four questions posted at the start turn out to have one answer. Cold became hunger when harvests failed and substitution ran out — the potato, banned in France until 1748 as pig food suspected of causing leprosy, was forced into the fields by Prussian famine policy in 1774 and became a northern staple. Who came through depended on whether reserves and trade were written down in advance: northeastern Japan's registers show mortality and flight climbing together in the 1780s Tenmei famine, while Kyushu in the south barely records it; Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. Neighbours under the same sky came out differently because provision was not evenly distributed. And what it left behind: England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure; the potato as insurance against grain failure; and in one Swiss village, a prayer against the glacier recited annually from the 1650s to the 1950s, now approved by Rome in reverse — asking the ice to stay.

The friar in Messina wrote down a sickness clinging to bones. The households buried in that emergency ground were laid out head to foot, with care. The cold lasted roughly 1300 to 1850. The village carried on. Fields were plowed. Bells were rung. Harvests were recorded.

The comfort of knowing why crops fail and having reserves written into law is strikingly new. For most of history, survival came down to whether someone had built the system before the cold arrived — not geography, not luck, but organisation.

Recorded as centuries of cold, but endured one winter and one harvest at a time.

弗朗切斯科会修士Michele da Piazza的同时代记录：'一场最致命的瘟疫在整个岛屿蔓延。事情发生在1347年10月初，大约12艘热那亚船只从神圣复仇中逃离（上帝因他们的罪而降下的），驶入墨西拿港，带来一种紧贴他们骨头的疾病'（bringing with them such a sickness clinging to their very bones）
英格兰赫特福德郡阿什韦尔（Ashwell）圣玛丽教堂塔内有1349-1350年刻字，内容被研究者描述为'不想让发生的事被遗忘'的证据。刻字提到'惨痛暴烈'（miseranda）、'狂暴'（ferox）、'只剩下平民作证'（plebs sola）等词
1642年夏蒙尼（Chamonix）地方官员记录：冰川从1641到1643年每年推进'一枪之距'（the distance of a gunshot），量化为每年75-150米，三年总计150-300米。1644年布瓦冰川（Glacier des Bois）几乎堵死整个山谷，有堵成湖的危险
黑死病后（1349年秋）英格兰农业劳动力成本显著上涨：东部、中部、南部各郡的小麦脱粒成本几乎翻倍，大麦和燕麦成本涨幅超过一倍。尽管1349-1350年《劳工法令》试图将工资压回1346年前水平，实际工资仍持续上涨
英格兰赫特福德郡阿什韦尔圣玛丽教堂塔内有1349-1350年刻字，研究者描述为不想让发生的事被遗忘的证据；柯里里维尔庄园法庭记录显示黑死病期间记录从日常琐事转为大量死亡并列出具体姓名和继承人；达勒姆圣尼古拉斯教区登记簿1540年9月开始记录洗礼、婚姻和埋葬，1597年记录'大瘟疫'死亡者名单，1587年记录玉米饥荒时的粮价清单
霍尔加思1号和3号庄园小屋的木材经树轮年代学测定返回伊丽莎白时期(1558-1603)和斯图亚特时期(1603-1714)的日期
西南兰开夏郡1558年看起来并非严重的死亡年份(教区登记簿保存较好的法恩沃思小教区未显示异常)，提示瘟疫确实局限于城市地区；1588年整个地区死亡率异常高；1590年代早期(1591-2年在多数地区，许多地区持续到1595年)再次出现困难时期
1590年代达勒姆地区高死亡率和粮食短缺之间存在明显关联，与国家层面研究者(Wrigley和Schofield)的发现形成对比——后者认为全国范围正向制约周期已消失，但他们也警告'使用全国数据时粮价对死亡率的影响看起来有限且不确定，并不否认在地方或区域层面可能发现粮食短缺造成毁灭性影响的清晰例子'
格雷斯托克教区1615-1627年婴儿死亡率数据显示：饥荒前后年均埋葬总数均为35人，1623年饥荒期间上升到164人(增加4.7倍)；1623年出生数降至23人，其中43%死亡；教区登记簿1620年12月至1622年6月关键时期缺失
研究者Appleby在分析1623年坎布里亚事件后提出'两个英格兰'论题：一个遭受贸易萧条和歉收但能够避免大规模饥饿，另一个(暗指偏远地区)在粮食短缺时面临更严重后果
格雷斯托克教区研究发现青少年生育力低下或青春期不育的良好证据，可能表明总体营养水平相当差；年龄别婚内生育率低，死产率高达9%(异常被记录在登记簿中)

全国范围1586年和1594-7年歉收，被描述为'本世纪最严重的连续歉收'

## Optimized Script

[CH01 | 0:00–2:49 | 现场开场与史料宣言：用一个当时记录者写下的、他自己也解释不了的一句话抓住观众，宣布接下来看的不是孤例而是有档案撑着的普通村子，再把标题问题拆成四个具体子问题挂出去]

October 1347, the start of the Little Ice Age. A harbour in Sicily, late autumn. Twelve Genoese galleys tying up at Messina after a long run from the east. A Franciscan friar in the town writes down one line about the men coming ashore.

They had brought with them a sickness clinging to their very bones.

He does not explain the phrase. He cannot. Within a year it will have travelled every trade road in Europe. For the next five hundred years, survival itself became the question. Everything that followed was written down. Not legend — records.

But this is not a film about that harbour.

It is about the kind of place nearly everyone actually lived in. One font. One wedding. One churchyard. A day's walk from a market. An English tenant household, farming land they did not own, paying rent in labour and in kind, tied to a manor court that recorded everything.

And about five hundred years of bad weather that were only just beginning there.

In the manor court rolls that tracked every tenant's death. In the tree rings that measured each growing season. In the emergency burial grounds archaeologists dug up centuries later.

So how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

That question splits into four.

First: how does cold turn into famine — and what interrupts that chain? A growing season shortens by a week or two — where does the hunger actually start?

Second: when harvests fail, what decides who survives? Luck, or something written down in advance?

Third: why do neighbouring places, under the same sky, come out so differently? One village loses a few families. Another loses half its population. What separates them?

Fourth: what did surviving communities build that others did not? In the economy. In the law. In the way people thought about survival itself.

So how long did this cold period last, how cold was it, and what did the world look like before it arrived?

[CH02 | 2:49–5:33 | 灾前基线：铺出寒冷的时间跨度与幅度、人口与土地压力的常态，并埋下一个琐碎的制度细节，明说后面会回来用它数人]

About five hundred and fifty years. From roughly 1300 to 1850.

The Little Ice Age cooled the northern hemisphere by under one degree Celsius. Tree rings and ice cores measure the drop by reading volcanic eruptions and solar output. Four volcanic eruptions before the cold began: the 1257 Samalas eruption, magnitude seven on the volcanic explosivity index, followed by three more between 1268 and 1284, then another pair in 1452 and 1453. Each threw sulphur into the stratosphere, reflecting sunlight back to space. Then four solar minima stretched across the centuries: the Wolf minimum, the Spörer, the Maunder minimum from 1645 to 1715, and the Dalton. Decades when sunspot counts dropped and solar output weakened.

One degree does not sound like much. But it shortened growing seasons, pushed the tree line lower, and turned marginal harvests into failed ones.

Now drop into the family that will carry this story. An English tenant household. Not nobility. Not the landless. The kind of family that held land from a manor, paid rent in labour, walked a day to reach the nearest market town.

By 1300, England held somewhere between four and five million people. Nearly all the land that could be plowed already was. Every strip had a name. Every harvest was spoken for. There was no reserve, no frontier, no empty valley to move into when things went wrong. The margin had closed.

When someone in this family died, the manor court recorded it. The lord's steward wrote down the tenant's name, the land they had held, and what the heir owed in heriot — the death duty. Usually a cow. Sometimes a horse. Occasionally a ram. A dull obligation. Bureaucratic routine.

But because the manor court wrote it down, historians centuries later can count the households that did not survive. That detail will matter.

People living through it had to explain the weather somehow — and they had recent experience to draw on. What did they think was happening, and what do we now know was happening?

[CH03 | 5:33–10:15 | 当时经验、双镜头认知对照与进入路径：先给上一次饥荒的记忆，再并置当时人的解释与今天的重建，承认科学内部仍有未决争论，然后白描寒冷怎么沿日常连接网进入村子、给出阻挡尝试和它的失败]

They had seen this before.

In the spring of 1315, the rain started and didn't stop. Through the summer, into autumn. The fields turned to mud. In Norfolk, grain went from five shillings per quarter to twenty. In Lorraine, wheat climbed three hundred and twenty percent. On August 10th, King Edward the Second passed through St Albans, and his own party could not buy bread. The shortage lasted years. Mortality in cities ran ten to twenty-five percent. Some regions lost more. Recovery took until the 1320s.

So when the cold returned, they already had a framework for what happens when harvests fail.

They blamed the stars. The University of Paris in 1348 issued a formal explanation: a conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars in Aquarius on March 20th, 1345, had drawn poisonous vapour from the earth and corrupted the air. The Church added divine punishment. Processions, prayer, fasting. Someone had to be at fault. In the coldest decades, accusations found targets. Between 1560 and 1698, the peaks in witch trials tracked the coldest years. In 1562, after a hailstorm destroyed the harvest near Wiesensteig, sixty-three women were burned.

Science now reads it differently.

Tree rings and ice cores record the physical drivers. Volcanic eruptions injecting sulphur, solar minimums weakening output. Researchers still argue over the weighting. A 2017 study of 43,000 trials across 21 countries found religious competition between Catholic and Protestant regions a stronger predictor than temperature. The mechanism remains unresolved.

What isn't disputed is that the cold arrived along routes the village already used.

The weekly market. The church court. The mill where grain was ground. Roads the priest walked, the miller's cart followed, the lord's steward travelled when collecting rents. The harbour that brought salt and wool and carried grain away. The village was not sealed off. Its survival required connection.

In the winter of 1683 to 1684, the Thames froze solid for two months. The ice held twenty-eight centimeters thick. Londoners built two streets of shops on the river: taverns, roast ox, bear-baiting. King Charles and his queen shared a portion. A printer set up a press on the ice, selling cards for sixpence with your name and the date. One printer took in five pounds a day. The diarist John Evelyn called it a Bacchanalian triumph on the river while on land it was severe judgment.

On January 23rd, 1795, the sea off Den Helder froze. A column of French hussars wrapped their horses' hooves in cloth, rode across the ice, and captured fourteen Dutch warships and eight hundred and fifty guns without firing a shot. Cavalry took a fleet.

The cold could reach that far.

And people tried to stop it. In the Chamonix valley, one Swiss village began an annual procession in the 1650s, walking up the mountain to pray that the glacier would not swallow their pastures. Every year for three centuries they asked. The ritual continued until the 1950s.

The glacier advanced anyway. From 1641 to 1643, the Bois glacier moved forward seventy-five to one hundred and fifty meters every year, nearly closing the valley.

It didn't work. Not because the villagers lacked effort or faith, but because what was arriving moved on a scale no procession could deflect.

So once it is inside the house, what does a winter like that actually feel like for the people in it?

[CH04 | 10:15–12:03 | 沉浸段：把宏观寒冷落进一间具体的屋子，看清居所结构、它在寒冷里的要害，以及人们硬撑过去的具体办法]

The house itself was timber frame with wattle-and-daub walls and a thatched roof. Most of the heat left through the walls and the thatch. An open hearth in the centre burned what wood the family could gather, but without a closed firebox most of the warmth went straight out through the roof.

Where fuel was abundant and building traditions different, the problem had been solved centuries earlier. In German-speaking regions and Scandinavia, the kachelofen — a tiled masonry stove — routed smoke through a maze of internal channels, holding the heat long after the fire went out. Fuel efficiency ran eighty to ninety percent, ten to twelve hours of warmth from two hours of burning. By the eighteenth century, wood shortages were severe enough that several governments funded improvements to stove design.

In Russia, the stove itself was the bed. Families built brick structures weighing over a ton, routing the smoke horizontally through a knee-shaped flue, and slept on top of it through the winter.

The English household in this film had none of that. They closed off most of the house for the season and lived in the kitchen. They hung curtains around the bed to trap body heat. They filled a long-handled copper warming pan with coals from the hearth and ran it between the sheets before climbing in. They wrapped heated stones and soapstone in cloth and kept them at their feet. At church, they brought their own foot stoves to survive the hour-long sermon. And they slept together — the entire household in one bed.

Heat you can arrange yourself. Food you cannot. When the harvest failed, who was supposed to feed this family?

[CH05 | 12:03–13:43 | 缺位与替代：列出正式供给顶不上来之后剩下的全部依靠，白描民间与政策各自拿出了什么，并评价这些办法里哪些真管用、哪些只是看着管用]

Largely no one. There was no state granary, no central relief, no assured supply. The answer was substitution — in the field and on the plate.

The crop that eventually underwrote northern diets had arrived in Europe in the mid-1500s and spent two centuries despised. The potato was pig food. France banned it outright in 1748 on suspicion it caused leprosy. What changed was famine. In 1744, Frederick the Great of Prussia issued it as military rations. In 1774, famine year, he ordered it planted across the kingdom and distributed free seed.

A French pharmacist named Parmentier had survived Prussian captivity on potatoes. He came home and spent decades promoting them. In 1772, the Paris medical faculty declared them edible. He planted a guarded field outside the city — guards by day, open by night. People came and stole the seedlings, as intended. He presented a potato flower to Louis XVI. By 1815, the potato was a northern staple.

Where there was nothing to substitute, people ate what they could. In Finland during the 1695–97 famine, that meant bark bread and wild ferns.

One of these worked. The other was just hunger with a recipe.

Where institutions held, the picture was different. Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged — its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure, built provision into statute before the next round arrived. In Japan's Tenmei famine of the 1780s, domains with community grain stores saw lower mortality than those without.

Substitution buys months. What happens when the pressure lasts long enough to bend the institutions themselves?

[CH06 | 13:43–15:39 | 制度承压：从纸面上出示一份权威机构书面让步核心规则的文件，说清它改了什么、为谁改、改到什么时候，并点明这种让步有多罕见]

The pressure kept building into 1349. Substitution had bought a few months. By January, the pressure had reached the institutions themselves — and the paperwork.

On January 23, 1349, Pope Clement VI issued a written directive. It concerned the last rite no one could do without: confession and absolution.

Under normal canon law, a dying person confessed to an ordained priest. Only a priest could grant absolution. The directive changed that. A plague victim facing death could now confess to any qualified confessor and receive absolution of all sins. That included laypeople — men with no ordination. If no man was available, it allowed confession to a woman.

The concession was valid until June 24, 1349 — the Feast of St. John the Baptist. The Church had written an expiry date into the emergency.

This is not a chronicle entry or a local bishop's improvisation. This is the papacy rewriting the procedure for the soul's final passage, putting the revision on paper, and setting a deadline for it to expire.

It is a rare thing to find an institution bending a rule this central. Rarer still to find it done in writing, with a date attached, as if the institution could budget for catastrophe the way it budgeted for jubilees.

The directive traveled through the dioceses. The Archbishop of York forwarded it to the Bishop of Carlisle and others. The rule had changed on paper.

If the rules broke down on paper, everything on the ground must have broken down too. Did it?

[CH07 | 15:39–17:15 | 体面反转：在观众预期最糟的地方摆出相反的实物证据，用现场细节推翻'极端压力下必然混乱'的想象，并提醒压力还在继续推进]

If the rules broke down on paper, you would expect the ground to give way completely. Bodies left where they fell. Households scattering without record. The kind of collapse that leaves no trace beyond the silence itself.

That is not what the excavations show.

An emergency burial ground excavated in England during the coldest years held forty-eight individuals. Over half of them were children. And they were still laid out head-to-foot in consistent alignment, as if the calendar had kept its ordinary shape even when nothing else did.

What caught the researchers was not the number. It was the arrangement.

Even under that much pressure, someone had taken the time to do it properly. The dead were not piled or abandoned. They were buried as neighbours, with the kind of care that does not show up in the death toll but says something about the people who kept going.

And the pressure did not stop there. The glacier kept advancing year after year. By the mid-seventeenth century, in some valleys the ice had almost sealed the passage shut.

If people under that much pressure stayed capable of care, then what made the difference between a village that lost a few and a village that lost half?

[CH08 | 17:15–18:30 | 论点反转：把同一场灾害里差别极大的两个地方并排放在一起，证明差别不在天气，并挂出一个留到结尾才收的疑问]

The answer is written in the registers.

In the 1780s and 1830s, when the Tenmei and Tenpō famines hit Japan, the records from northeastern villages show mortality and flight climbing together. In Hirosaki domain, the population loss approached half. Same sky, different archives. In the south, Kyushu records barely register the famines at all. The northeastern villages had no grain reserves written into law. Kyushu domains had community stores built decades earlier.

Same decades. Opposite outcomes. The difference was not weather. It was what had been organized before the weather turned.

And this pattern holds across oceans. When famine spread across Europe in the 1590s, Amsterdam came through with the least damage. Not because the weather was kinder there. Because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing when inland cities starved.

England's 1598 Poor Law is read by researchers today as a written adaptation to climate pressure. Provision built into statute before the next round arrived.

The difference was not latitude. It was organisation. One village had written down who would be fed and how. Another had not.

But that is a claim about structure. Can we actually count the dead household by household and check it?

[CH09 | 18:30–21:32 | 计数：展示基层记录机构的日常职能如何从琐事转为灾祸，给出有名有姓的个案，用方法论说明枯燥文书为何可信，再收在总量与地区差异上]

We can. Because every death left a written trail.

The manor court at Curry Rivel in Somerset held sessions three times a year. Most of what it recorded was dull estate business: who violated the ale laws, who let a hedge fall, who owed the lord a day's plowing. In the sessions before 1348, the rolls list tenants by name for breaking regulations.

Then the rolls change.

John Patel held a tenement. Heriot recorded. His heir: Alice, his daughter.

Ralph Echeman held land. His heir: Adam, his son.

Walter Springold held part of a tenement and two and a half acres. Heriot recorded. His heir: Robert, his brother.

Three names. Three inheritances recorded between spring and autumn 1349.

This is what makes counting possible. The manor court recorded deaths because the lord collected heriot — the death duty we saw at the start. A transaction between lord and heir, written into the rolls so the account would stand. That dull administrative obligation is what lets historians today count the households that did not make it through.

Multiply Curry Rivel across the parishes with surviving records. Historians studying the 1348-1350 epidemic have estimated mortality at one third to one half of the population in England.

The coldest stretches killed in different measures. Finland's 1695-97 famine took roughly 150,000 out of 500,000 — close to one third. Iceland's Laki eruption in 1783 and the famine that followed claimed about one fifth: 9,000 to 10,000 people. Japan's Tenmei famine cost Hirosaki domain nearly half.

In 1639, a county gazetteer in Shandong recorded: "From first month no rain to sixth month, seventh month great locusts, the year greatly hungry, people ate people, wanderers filled the roads."

In the winter of 1709, possibly the coldest Europe had seen in five hundred years, an estimated 500,000 people in France died of hunger and malnutrition.

The scale varied by region, by decade, by what reserves had been laid down before the cold arrived. But the structure of the counting is the same. A tenant dies. The court records the heriot. The heir takes the holding. Or the holding stands empty, and that too goes into the roll.

And for the ones still standing in the spring — did life get worse, or did something change in their favour?

[CH10 | 21:32–25:35 | 灾后景象与后果链：用不等人的转折建立紧迫感，排比空置与静默的意象，给出供需关系反过来的具体表现，展示权力方的压制与压制的失败，再给出几十年尺度的后续证据]

The ground keeps its own calendar.

Spring 1350. The fields need plowing whether the village has enough hands or not. The seedtime does not wait for the parish to recover. And when the surviving families walked their strips that March, they walked past holdings no one had claimed. Fewer men sitting the benches in the manor court. Fewer carts on the road to market. Voices missing from the choir.

For the first time in living memory, the problem was not too many people and too little land.

It was the other way around.

The cost of getting work done flipped. Before the plague, a man holding a quarter-virgate worked his lord's strips two or three days a week as rent, and counted himself lucky to hold anything at all. After, the same man could look at twenty empty holdings and ask: what will you pay me to thresh your wheat?

The account rolls record the new arithmetic. In England, the cost of threshing wheat nearly doubled between the 1340s and the early 1350s. Barley and oats — the cost more than doubled. The work was the same. The grain was the same. The number of people able to swing a flail had dropped by a third or more, and every lord with a harvest needed them.

The crown knew it too.

Autumn 1349. Before the plague year was even finished, the English government issued an ordinance fixing wages at the levels paid in 1346. Any labourer or artisan demanding more — named penalties. Any employer paying more — fined.

The account books show what happened.

The law named the rates. The shortage overrode them.

It could not change basic arithmetic. There were far fewer people, but just as much land. Just as many fields to plow, just as much grain to thresh, just as many roofs to mend. Within five years, the lords who had legislated the wage ceiling were paying above it themselves, or watching their harvest rot.

And over the following decades, the structure began to shift. Labour services — the two or three days a week a tenant owed his lord — converted to cash rents. Tenants who had been tied to a holding by custom and law found the lord suddenly willing to negotiate. By the 1370s, villeins were bargaining. By the 1380s, some were walking off holdings their families had worked for generations, because another manor down the road would pay more or ask less.

The long-term consequence was not immediate collapse. It was a slow loosening of the bonds that had held the manor system in place since before anyone could remember. Tenants who had inherited unfree status found the lord less interested in enforcing it when he needed hands. Courts that had once fined a villein for leaving without permission began letting it slide. Cash replaced obligation. Mobility replaced fixity.

And in June 1381, thirty years after the first plague summer, a tax revolt in Essex became a march on London, and the Peasants' Revolt burned the records in the Tower. The men who led it had grown up in the world the plague had left behind — a world where labour knew its value, and the law that said otherwise had already lost.

Everyone has heard that whole villages were simply wiped off the map. Is that what the records show?

[CH11 | 25:35–26:46 | 流行说法纠偏：显式引用一个人人听过的说法，用一个确实符合它的个案承认它部分成立，再用更大范围的证据重定主因，最后用罕见与常见的定性收口]

The common version: whole villages vanished.

That did happen. In the Chamonix valley in the French Alps, at least six villages were flattened by advancing glaciers between 1600 and 1650. In 1642, local officials recorded ice moving forward daily, carrying off houses and livestock. By 1644, the Bois glacier had nearly sealed the valley.

But most places that emptied out didn't vanish in a season. The Norse Greenland colony's western settlement was abandoned around 1350, its eastern settlement around the mid-1400s. The last written record is a 1408 church wedding. It took generations. Sea ice closed the harbours. Pasture shrank. Trade lines died. The colony bled out slowly.

Meanwhile, the Inuit living in the same ice did well — kayaks, harpoons, sealskin clothing.

Total erasure was rare. Long attrition was the norm.

All of this is us reading their paperwork. Did anyone living through it leave words of their own?

[CH12 | 26:46–28:37 | 当事人的声音与回袭序列：说明直接声音有多稀缺，出示留下来的直接证物及其内容，对作者身份保持开放，再给出灾害反复回袭的时间序列和恢复的尺度]

Records written about people. But what about words written by them?

Direct testimony from inside these years is rare. Most who lived through it left nothing. What survives is administrative — court rolls, tax lists, wills. But there are two exceptions.

In Ashwell, Hertfordshire, inside the tower of St Mary's church, someone carved words into the stone sometime between 1349 and 1350. The inscription includes three Latin words: miseranda — lamentable. Ferox — violent. And plebs sola — only the common people remain to witness.

We don't know who held the chisel. Researchers interpret it: a witness determined to preserve what they saw.

That's one voice, anonymous.

The other is named. In Iceland, a pastor named Jón Steingrímsson kept a day-by-day record through the 1783 Laki eruption — the same eruption that fed into the Tenmei famine. His account documents the sulphur haze, the livestock deaths, the famine that followed. Local tradition says his 'Fire Sermon' stopped the advancing lava at the village edge.

And the cold years kept returning. The plague came back in 1361, 1369, and 1375. Finland lost a third of its population in 1695 to 1697. The winter of 1709 froze Europe so hard that wine solidified in cellars and trees split open. In 1816, New York saw snow on 6 June. Pennsylvania rivers froze in August.

How long did full recovery take? When, if ever, did the recurrences stop?

Why was it this deadly, and what did it leave behind that is still standing today?

[CH13 | 28:37–30:45 | 归因与政治代价：抛出'为什么这么致命'的问句，给出谁更容易被选中的证据，追溯一条政治后果链从饥荒到国家失去独立]

Why was it this deadly?

Part of the answer is arithmetic. The societies that paid the highest price were the ones with the least to fall back on when the harvests failed: no grain reserves written down in advance, no trade networks to bring supply in from outside, no provision system to keep the most vulnerable alive through the spring.

The bill was not only in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years, from 1695 to 1699, killed between 10 and 15 per cent of the population. The famine drove a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. Scotland staked about a fifth of its national capital on a colony at the Panama isthmus. Three thousand settlers sailed in 1698. Two thousand died within two years. The scheme collapsed, and its failure put direct pressure on the 1707 union with England. One famine decade rewrote the constitutional map.

Other states missed the recovery window by years. Tree-ring reconstructions show temperatures returned to the long-run mean by 1650. The Ming dynasty fell in 1644, six years before that threshold. The climatic pressure lifted just as the state gave way. Had the recovery come earlier, the outcome might have been different. But it did not.

The cold did not choose its victims at random. It killed where there was no system to interrupt the chain from harvest failure to starvation, and where there was no capital cushion to survive a failed bet.

So, in one sentence: how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

[CH14 | 30:45–33:00 | 逐问回收与结尾回扣：召回标题问句，逐条收束开场挂起的子问题，补上制度遗产，用延续下去的画面反转最惊人的定性，相对化今天的安全感，再以一句对照收尾]

They survived by organising before the crisis arrived.

The four questions posted at the start turn out to have one answer. Cold became hunger when harvests failed and substitution ran out — the potato, banned in France until 1748 as pig food suspected of causing leprosy, was forced into the fields by Prussian famine policy in 1774 and became a northern staple. Who came through depended on whether reserves and trade were written down in advance: northeastern Japan's registers show mortality and flight climbing together in the 1780s Tenmei famine, while Kyushu in the south barely records it; Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. Neighbours under the same sky came out differently because provision was not evenly distributed. And what it left behind: England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure; the potato as insurance against grain failure; and in one Swiss village, a prayer against the glacier recited annually from the 1650s to the 1950s, now approved by Rome in reverse — asking the ice to stay.

The friar in Messina wrote down a sickness clinging to bones. The households buried in that emergency ground were laid out head to foot, with care. The cold lasted roughly 1300 to 1850. The village carried on. Fields were plowed. Bells were rung. Harvests were recorded.

The comfort of knowing why crops fail and having reserves written into law is strikingly new. For most of history, survival came down to whether someone had built the system before the cold arrived — not geography, not luck, but organisation.

Recorded as centuries of cold, but endured one winter and one harvest at a time.
