[CH01 | 0:00–2:49 | 现场开场与史料宣言：用一个当时记录者写下的、他自己也解释不了的一句话抓住观众，宣布接下来看的不是孤例而是有档案撑着的普通村子，再把标题问题拆成四个具体子问题挂出去]

October 1347, the start of the Little Ice Age. A harbour in Sicily, late autumn. Twelve Genoese galleys tying up at Messina after a long run from the east. A Franciscan friar in the town writes down one line about the men coming ashore.

They had brought with them a sickness clinging to their very bones.

He does not explain the phrase. He cannot. Within a year it will have travelled every trade road in Europe. For the next five hundred years, survival itself became the question. Everything that followed was written down. Not legend — records.

But this is not a film about that harbour.

It is about the kind of place nearly everyone actually lived in. One font. One wedding. One churchyard. A day's walk from a market. An English tenant household, farming land they did not own, paying rent in labour and in kind, tied to a manor court that recorded everything.

And about five hundred years of bad weather that were only just beginning there.

In the manor court rolls that tracked every tenant's death. In the tree rings that measured each growing season. In the emergency burial grounds archaeologists dug up centuries later.

So how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

That question splits into four.

First: how does cold turn into famine — and what interrupts that chain? A growing season shortens by a week or two — where does the hunger actually start?

Second: when harvests fail, what decides who survives? Luck, or something written down in advance?

Third: why do neighbouring places, under the same sky, come out so differently? One village loses a few families. Another loses half its population. What separates them?

Fourth: what did surviving communities build that others did not? In the economy. In the law. In the way people thought about survival itself.

So how long did this cold period last, how cold was it, and what did the world look like before it arrived?

[CH02 | 2:49–5:33 | 灾前基线：铺出寒冷的时间跨度与幅度、人口与土地压力的常态，并埋下一个琐碎的制度细节，明说后面会回来用它数人]

Decades when sunspot counts dropped and solar output weakened.

When someone in this family died, the manor court recorded it. The lord's steward wrote down the tenant's name, the land they had held, and what the heir owed in heriot — the death duty. Usually a cow. Sometimes a horse. Occasionally a ram. A dull obligation. Bureaucratic routine.

But because the manor court wrote it down, historians centuries later can count the households that did not survive. That detail will matter.

People living through it had to explain the weather somehow — and they had recent experience to draw on. What did they think was happening, and what do we now know was happening?

[CH03 | 5:33–10:15 | 当时经验、双镜头认知对照与进入路径：先给上一次饥荒的记忆，再并置当时人的解释与今天的重建，承认科学内部仍有未决争论，然后白描寒冷怎么沿日常连接网进入村子、给出阻挡尝试和它的失败]

They had seen this before.

In the spring of 1315, the rain started and didn't stop. Through the summer, into autumn. The fields turned to mud. In Norfolk, grain went from five shillings per quarter to twenty. The shortage lasted years. Mortality in cities ran ten to twenty-five percent. Some regions lost more. Recovery took until the 1320s.

They blamed the stars. The University of Paris in 1348 issued a formal explanation: a conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars in Aquarius in the 1340s had drawn poisonous vapour from the earth and corrupted the air. What isn't disputed is that the cold arrived along routes the village already used.

The weekly market. The church court. The mill where grain was ground. Roads the priest walked, the miller's cart followed, the lord's steward travelled when collecting rents. The harbour that brought salt and wool and carried grain away. The village was not sealed off. Its survival required connection.

In the winter of 1683 to 1684, the Thames froze solid for two months. Londoners built two streets of shops on the river: taverns, roast ox, bear-baiting. King Charles and his queen shared a portion. A printer set up a press on the ice, selling cards for sixpence with your name and the date. One printer took in five pounds a day. The diarist John Evelyn called it a Bacchanalian triumph on the river while on land it was severe judgment.

On January 23rd, 1795, the sea off Den Helder froze. A column of French hussars wrapped their horses' hooves in cloth, rode across the ice, and captured fourteen Dutch warships without firing a shot. Cavalry took a fleet.

The cold could reach that far.

And people tried to stop it. In the Chamonix valley, one Swiss village began an annual procession in the 1650s, walking up the mountain to pray that the glacier would not swallow their pastures. Every year for three centuries they asked.

The glacier advanced anyway. From 1641 to 1643, the Bois glacier moved forward seventy-five to one hundred and fifty meters every year, nearly closing the valley.

It didn't work. Not because the villagers lacked effort or faith, but because what was arriving moved on a scale no procession could deflect.

So once it is inside the house, what does a winter like that actually feel like for the people in it?

[CH04 | 10:15–12:03 | 沉浸段：把宏观寒冷落进一间具体的屋子，看清居所结构、它在寒冷里的要害，以及人们硬撑过去的具体办法]

The house itself was timber frame with wattle-and-daub walls and a thatched roof. Most of the heat left through the walls and the thatch. An open hearth in the centre burned what wood the family could gather, but without a closed firebox most of the warmth went straight out through the roof.

Where fuel was abundant and building traditions different, the problem had been solved centuries earlier. In German-speaking regions and Scandinavia, the kachelofen — a tiled masonry stove — routed smoke through a maze of internal channels, holding the heat long after the fire went out. Two hours of burning gave ten to twelve hours of warmth. By the eighteenth century, wood shortages were severe enough that several governments funded improvements to stove design.

In Russia, the stove itself was the bed. Families built brick structures weighing over a ton, routing the smoke horizontally through a knee-shaped flue, and slept on top of it through the winter.

The English household in this film had none of that. They closed off most of the house for the season and lived in the kitchen. They hung curtains around the bed to trap body heat. They filled a long-handled copper warming pan with coals from the hearth and ran it between the sheets before climbing in. They wrapped heated stones and soapstone in cloth and kept them at their feet. At church, they brought their own foot stoves to survive the hour-long sermon. And they slept together — the entire household in one bed.

Heat you can arrange yourself. Food you cannot. When the harvest failed, who was supposed to feed this family?

[CH05 | 12:03–13:43 | 缺位与替代：列出正式供给顶不上来之后剩下的全部依靠，白描民间与政策各自拿出了什么，并评价这些办法里哪些真管用、哪些只是看着管用]

Largely no one. There was no state granary, no central relief, no assured supply. The answer was substitution — in the field and on the plate.

The crop that eventually underwrote northern diets had arrived in Europe in the mid-1500s and spent two centuries despised. The potato was pig food. France banned it outright in 1748 on suspicion it caused leprosy. What changed was famine. In 1744, Frederick the Great of Prussia issued it as military rations. In 1774, famine year, he ordered it planted across the kingdom and distributed free seed.

A French pharmacist named Parmentier had survived Prussian captivity on potatoes. He came home and spent decades promoting them. In 1772, the Paris medical faculty declared them edible. He planted a guarded field outside the city — guards by day, open by night. People came and stole the seedlings, as intended. He presented a potato flower to Louis XVI. By 1815, the potato was a northern staple.

Where there was nothing to substitute, people ate what they could. In Finland during the 1695–97 famine, that meant bark bread and wild ferns.

One of these worked. The other was just hunger with a recipe.

Where institutions held, the picture was different. Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged — its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure, built provision into statute before the next round arrived. In Japan's Tenmei famine of the 1780s, domains with community grain stores saw lower mortality than those without.

Substitution buys months. What happens when the pressure lasts long enough to bend the institutions themselves?

[CH06 | 13:43–15:39 | 制度承压：从纸面上出示一份权威机构书面让步核心规则的文件，说清它改了什么、为谁改、改到什么时候，并点明这种让步有多罕见]

The pressure kept building into 1349. Substitution had bought a few months. By that winter, the pressure had reached the institutions themselves — and the paperwork.

In 1349, Pope Clement VI issued directives concerning the last rite no one could do without: confession and absolution.

Under normal canon law, a dying person confessed to an ordained priest. Only a priest could grant absolution. The directive changed that. A plague victim facing death could now confess to any qualified confessor and receive absolution of all sins. That included laypeople — men with no ordination. If no man was available, it allowed confession to a woman.

This is not a chronicle entry or a local bishop's improvisation. This is the papacy adjusting the procedure for the soul's final passage and putting the adjustment on paper during the emergency.

It is a rare thing to find an institution bending a rule this central. Rarer still to find it done in writing as if the institution could budget for catastrophe the way it budgeted for jubilees.

The directive traveled through the dioceses. The Archbishop of York forwarded it to the Bishop of Carlisle and others. The rule had changed on paper.

If the rules broke down on paper, everything on the ground must have broken down too. Did it?

[CH07 | 15:39–17:15 | 体面反转：在观众预期最糟的地方摆出相反的实物证据，用现场细节推翻'极端压力下必然混乱'的想象，并提醒压力还在继续推进]

If the rules broke down on paper, you would expect the ground to give way completely. Bodies left where they fell. Households scattering without record. The kind of collapse that leaves no trace beyond the silence itself.

That is not what the excavations show.

Emergency burial grounds excavated in England from the plague years held organized burials. In one cemetery, researchers found individuals still laid out head-to-foot in consistent alignment, as if the calendar had kept its ordinary shape even when nothing else did.

What caught the researchers was not the number. It was the arrangement.

Even under that much pressure, someone had taken the time to do it properly. The dead were not piled or abandoned. They were buried as neighbours, with the kind of care that does not show up in the death toll but says something about the people who kept going.

And the pressure did not stop there. The glacier kept advancing year after year. By the mid-seventeenth century, in some valleys the ice had almost sealed the passage shut.

If people under that much pressure stayed capable of care, then what made the difference between a village that lost a few and a village that lost half?

[CH08 | 17:15–18:30 | 论点反转：把同一场灾害里差别极大的两个地方并排放在一起，证明差别不在天气，并挂出一个留到结尾才收的疑问]

The answer is written in the registers.

In the 1780s and 1830s, when the Tenmei and Tenpō famines hit Japan, the records from northeastern villages show mortality and flight climbing together. In Hirosaki domain, the population loss approached half. Same sky, different archives. In the south, Kyushu records barely register the famines at all.

Same decades. Opposite outcomes. The difference was not weather.

And this pattern holds across oceans. When famine spread across Europe in the 1590s, Amsterdam came through with the least damage. Not because the weather was kinder there. Because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing when inland cities starved.

England's 1598 Poor Law is read by researchers today as a written adaptation to climate pressure. Provision built into statute before the next round arrived.

The difference was not latitude. It was what had been organized before the cold arrived. One place had built reserves and trade networks in advance. Another had not.

But that is a claim about structure. Can we actually count the dead household by household and check it?

[CH09 | 18:30–21:32 | 计数：展示基层记录机构的日常职能如何从琐事转为灾祸，给出有名有姓的个案，用方法论说明枯燥文书为何可信，再收在总量与地区差异上]

We can. Because every death left a written trail.

The manor court at Curry Rivel in Somerset held sessions three times a year. Most of what it recorded was dull estate business: who violated the ale laws, who let a hedge fall, who owed the lord a day's plowing. In the sessions before 1348, the rolls list tenants by name for breaking regulations.

Then the rolls change.

Manor court rolls from Curry Rivel record deaths and heirs during 1348-1349, with heriot payments and inheritance listed. The steward wrote down who had died, what land they held, what was owed to the lord at death, and who inherited.

This is what makes counting possible. The manor court recorded deaths because the lord collected heriot — the death duty we saw at the start. A transaction between lord and heir, written into the rolls so the account would stand. That dull administrative obligation is what lets historians today count the households that did not make it through.

Multiply Curry Rivel across the parishes with surviving records. Historians studying the 1348-1350 epidemic have estimated mortality at one third to one half of the population in England.

The coldest stretches killed in different measures. Finland's 1695-97 famine is estimated to have taken roughly one third of the population. Iceland's Laki eruption in 1783 and the famine that followed took a heavy toll. Japan's Tenmei famine cost Hirosaki domain nearly half.

In 1639, a county gazetteer in Shandong recorded: "From first month no rain to sixth month, seventh month great locusts, the year greatly hungry, people ate people, wanderers filled the roads."

The scale varied by region, by decade, by what reserves had been laid down before the cold arrived. But the structure of the counting is the same. A tenant dies. The court records the heriot. The heir takes the holding. Or the holding stands empty, and that too goes into the roll.

And for the ones still standing in the spring — did life get worse, or did something change in their favour?

[CH10 | 21:32–25:35 | 灾后景象与后果链：用不等人的转折建立紧迫感，排比空置与静默的意象，给出供需关系反过来的具体表现，展示权力方的压制与压制的失败，再给出几十年尺度的后续证据]

The ground keeps its own calendar.

Spring 1350. The fields need plowing whether the village has enough hands or not. The seedtime does not wait for the parish to recover. And when the surviving families walked their strips that March, they walked past holdings no one had claimed. Fewer men sitting the benches in the manor court. Fewer carts on the road to market. Voices missing from the choir.

For the first time in living memory, the problem was not too many people and too little land.

It was the other way around.

The cost of getting work done flipped. Before the plague, a man holding a quarter-virgate worked his lord's strips two or three days a week as rent, and counted himself lucky to hold anything at all. After, the same man could look at twenty empty holdings and ask: what will you pay me to thresh your wheat?

The account rolls record the new arithmetic. Agricultural labor costs rose sharply after the Black Death. The work was the same. The grain was the same. The number of people able to swing a flail had dropped by a third or more, and every lord with a harvest needed them.

The crown knew it too.

In 1349, English authorities issued wage ordinances attempting to fix labor costs. Any labourer or artisan demanding more — named penalties. Any employer paying more — fined.

The account books show what happened.

The law named the rates. The shortage overrode them.

Fewer hands, same amount of land. Same fields to plow, same grain to thresh, same roofs to mend. Within five years, the lords who had legislated the wage ceiling were paying above it themselves, or watching their harvest rot.

And over the following decades, the structure began to shift. Labour services — the two or three days a week a tenant owed his lord — converted to cash rents. Tenants who had been tied to a holding by custom and law found the lord suddenly willing to negotiate. By the 1370s, villeins were bargaining. By the early 1380s, some were walking off holdings their families had worked for generations, because another manor down the road would pay more or ask less.

The long-term consequence was not immediate collapse. It was a slow loosening of the bonds that had held the manor system in place since before anyone could remember. Tenants who had inherited unfree status found the lord less interested in enforcing it when he needed hands. Courts that had once fined a villein for leaving without permission began letting it slide. Cash replaced obligation. Mobility replaced fixity.

And in June 1381, thirty years after the first plague summer, a tax revolt in Essex became a march on London, and the Peasants' Revolt burned the records in the Tower. The men who led it had grown up in the world the plague had left behind — a world where labour knew its value, and the law that said otherwise had already lost.

Everyone has heard that whole villages were simply wiped off the map. Is that what the records show?

[CH11 | 25:35–26:46 | 流行说法纠偏：显式引用一个人人听过的说法，用一个确实符合它的个案承认它部分成立，再用更大范围的证据重定主因，最后用罕见与常见的定性收口]

The common version: whole villages vanished.

That did happen. In the Chamonix valley in the French Alps, at least six villages were flattened by advancing glaciers between 1600 and 1650. In 1642, local officials recorded ice moving forward daily, carrying off houses and livestock. By 1644, the Bois glacier had nearly sealed the valley.

But most places that emptied out didn't vanish in a season. The Norse Greenland colony's western settlement was abandoned around 1350, its eastern settlement sometime in the fifteenth century. It took generations. Sea ice closed the harbours. Pasture shrank. Trade lines died. The colony bled out slowly.

Meanwhile, the Inuit living in the same ice did well — kayaks, harpoons, sealskin clothing.

Total erasure was rare. Long attrition was the norm.

All of this is us reading their paperwork. Did anyone living through it leave words of their own?

[CH12 | 26:46–28:37 | 当事人的声音与回袭序列：说明直接声音有多稀缺，出示留下来的直接证物及其内容，对作者身份保持开放，再给出灾害反复回袭的时间序列和恢复的尺度]

Records written about people. But what about words written by them?

Direct testimony from inside these years is rare. Most who lived through it left nothing. What survives is administrative — court rolls, tax lists, wills. But there are two exceptions.

In Ashwell, Hertfordshire, inside the tower of St Mary's church, someone carved words into the stone sometime between 1349 and 1350. Researchers describe the inscription as a determination not to let what happened be forgotten.

We don't know who held the chisel.

That's one voice, anonymous.

The other is named. In Iceland, a pastor named Jón Steingrímsson kept a day-by-day record through the 1783 Laki eruption — the same eruption that fed into the Tenmei famine. His account documents the sulphur haze, the livestock deaths, the famine that followed. Local tradition says his 'Fire Sermon' stopped the advancing lava at the village edge.

And the cold years kept returning. The plague came back in repeated outbreaks through the 1360s and 1370s. Finland lost a third of its population in 1695 to 1697. The winter of 1709 froze Europe so hard that wine solidified in cellars and trees split open. In 1816, New York saw snow in June. Pennsylvania rivers froze in August.

Recovery took generations. The population levels of 1300 were not reached again until well into the sixteenth century.

Why was it this deadly, and what did it leave behind that is still standing today?

[CH13 | 28:37–30:45 | 归因与政治代价：抛出'为什么这么致命'的问句，给出谁更容易被选中的证据，追溯一条政治后果链从饥荒到国家失去独立]

Why was it this deadly?

Part of the answer is arithmetic. The societies that paid the highest price were the ones with the least to fall back on when the harvests failed: no grain reserves written down in advance, no trade networks to bring supply in from outside, no provision system to keep the most vulnerable alive through the spring.

The bill was not only in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years, from 1695 to 1699, devastated the population. The famine drove a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. Scotland staked about a fifth of its national capital on a colony at the Panama isthmus. Three thousand settlers sailed in 1698. Two thousand died within two years. The scheme collapsed, and its failure put direct pressure on the 1707 union with England. One famine decade rewrote the constitutional map.

Other states missed the recovery window by years. Tree-ring reconstructions suggest temperatures returned toward historical averages by 1650. The Ming dynasty fell in 1644, six years before that threshold. The climatic pressure lifted just as the state gave way. Had the recovery come earlier, the outcome might have been different. But it did not.

The cold did not choose its victims at random. It killed where there was no system to interrupt the chain from harvest failure to starvation, and where there was no capital cushion to survive a failed bet.

So, in one sentence: how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

[CH14 | 30:45–33:00 | 逐问回收与结尾回扣：召回标题问句，逐条收束开场挂起的子问题，补上制度遗产，用延续下去的画面反转最惊人的定性，相对化今天的安全感，再以一句对照收尾]

They survived by organising before the crisis arrived.

The four questions posted at the start turn out to have one answer. Cold became hunger when harvests failed and substitution ran out — the potato, banned in France until 1748 as pig food suspected of causing leprosy, was forced into the fields by Prussian famine policy in 1774 and became a northern staple. Who came through depended on whether reserves and trade were written down in advance: northeastern Japan's registers show mortality and flight climbing together in the 1780s Tenmei famine, while Kyushu in the south barely records it; Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. Neighbours under the same sky came out differently because provision was not evenly distributed. And what it left behind: England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure; the potato as insurance against grain failure; and in one Swiss village, a prayer against the glacier recited annually from the 1650s into the twentieth century, now approved by Rome in reverse — asking the ice to stay.

The friar in Messina wrote down a sickness clinging to bones. The households buried in that emergency ground were laid out head to foot, with care. The cold lasted from roughly the fourteenth century to the mid-nineteenth. The village carried on. Fields were plowed. Bells were rung. Harvests were recorded.

The comfort of knowing why crops fail and having reserves written into law is strikingly new. For most of history, what helped people survive was never luck or a warmer latitude. It was the system someone had built before the cold arrived.

versions.text:
[CH01 | 0:00–2:49 | 现场开场与史料宣言：用一个当时记录者写下的、他自己也解释不了的一句话抓住观众，宣布接下来看的不是孤例而是有档案撑着的普通村子，再把标题问题拆成四个具体子问题挂出去]

Spring 1315. In northern Europe, the rain began and kept falling. Fields turned to mud. Grain prices rose as harvests failed. This was the start of a famine that would expose a harder question: when cold and rain threaten the harvest, what helps a household survive? The answer is recorded in court rolls, grain prices, tree rings, and the abandoned places left behind.

It is about the kind of place nearly everyone actually lived in. One font. One wedding. One churchyard. A day's walk from a market. An English tenant household, farming land they did not own, paying rent in labour and in kind, tied to a manor court that recorded everything.

And about five hundred years of bad weather that were only just beginning there.

In manor court rolls that recorded tenants and inheritances. In tree rings that measured growing seasons. In grain prices and the remains of places abandoned as conditions changed.

So how did people survive the Little Ice Age?

That question splits into four.

First, in the famine chain: how does bad weather become hunger, and what can interrupt it?

Second, when harvests fail, what helps a household get through: luck, or support already in place?

Third, why do nearby regions sometimes suffer differently under the same broad climate pressures?

And fourth, what did communities build that helped them face the next shortage?

To answer those questions, start with the period's scale and the pressures people already faced.

[CH02 | 2:49–5:33 | 灾前基线：铺出寒冷的时间跨度与幅度、人口与土地压力的常态，并埋下一个琐碎的制度细节，明说后面会回来用它数人]

About five and a half centuries. From roughly the fourteenth to the mid-nineteenth century — scholars differ on when exactly it began.

The Little Ice Age cooled the northern hemisphere by under one degree Celsius. Tree rings and ice cores help reconstruct the climate. Major volcanic eruptions, including Samalas in 1257 and another in the 1450s, pushed conditions colder by sending sulphur into the atmosphere, where it reflected sunlight. Several periods of low solar activity also stretched across these centuries, including the Maunder minimum from 1645 to 1715.

In Finland during the 1695–97 famine, that meant bark bread and wild ferns.

One of these worked. The other was just hunger with a recipe.
issues.fix: In Finland during the 1695–97 famine, people ate bark bread and wild ferns. Neither could replace grain; both were emergency foods people turned to when ordinary supplies failed.

issues.problem: 保留账本支持的贸易和济贫法材料，将日本地区结果与未经证实的义仓因果机制分开，避免把相关性说成已证实的制度效果。
issues.quote: Where institutions held, the picture was different. Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged — its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure, built provision into statute before the next round arrived. In Japan's Tenmei famine of the 1780s, domains with community grain stores saw lower mortality than those without.
issues.fix: Trade and public provision could also buffer shortages. In the 1590s famine, Amsterdam's Baltic grain trade helped keep supplies flowing. Researchers read England's 1598 Poor Law as an institutional response to climate pressure. The Japanese records show sharply different regional outcomes during the Tenmei famine; they do not, by themselves, establish how a particular grain-store system worked.

issues.problem: 原段教皇教令、告解与瘟疫压力均不属于小冰期饥荒论证。改用账本中的济贫法研究解读，承接替代食物与制度性应对。
issues.quote:
The pressure kept building into 1349. Substitution had bought a few months. By that winter, the pressure had reached the institutions themselves — and the paperwork.

In 1349, Pope Clement VI issued directives concerning the last rite no one could do without: confession and absolution.

Under normal canon law, a dying person confessed to an ordained priest. Only a priest could grant absolution. The directive changed that. A plague victim facing death could now confess to any qualified confessor and receive absolution of all sins. That included laypeople — men with no ordination. If no man was available, it allowed confession to a woman.

This is not a chronicle entry or a local bishop's improvisation. This is the papacy adjusting the procedure for the soul's final passage and putting the adjustment on paper during the emergency.

It is a rare thing to find an institution bending a rule this central. Rarer still to find it done in writing as if the institution could budget for catastrophe the way it budgeted for jubilees.

The directive traveled through the dioceses. The Archbishop of York forwarded it to the Bishop of Carlisle and others. The rule had changed on paper.

If the rules broke down on paper, everything on the ground must have broken down too. Did it?
issues.fix: The question now moves from emergency food to lasting provision. In England, researchers interpret the 1598 Poor Law as one institutional response to climate pressure: support was written into law rather than left entirely to a household's luck. That does not mean relief could prevent every death. It means a community could make provision before the next shortage arrived.

issues.problem: 原段用黑死病墓地考古证明小冰期时期的照护与秩序，证据错配。改为现有日本地区记录，并明确其不能单独证明具体制度因果。
issues.quote:
If the rules broke down on paper, you would expect the ground to give way completely. Bodies left where they fell. Households scattering without record. The kind of collapse that leaves no trace beyond the silence itself.

That is not what the excavations show.

Emergency burial grounds excavated in England from the plague years held organized burials. In one cemetery, researchers found individuals still laid out head-to-foot in consistent alignment, as if the calendar had kept its ordinary shape even when nothing else did.

What caught the researchers was not the number. It was the arrangement.

Even under that much pressure, someone had taken the time to do it properly. The dead were not piled or abandoned. They were buried as neighbours, with the kind of care that does not show up in the death toll but says something about the people who kept going.
issues.fix: But a written policy is not the same as food in a household's hands. The Japanese records give us a different kind of comparison: during the Tenmei and Tenpō famines, northeastern records show mortality and flight rising together, while accounts from Kyushu contain little trace of famine deaths. The contrast matters, but it does not tell us on its own which local institutions produced it.

issues.problem: 原文继续用冰川和瘟疫式“照护反转”延伸不相关论证。改后承接日本对照，明确进入证据与因果边界。
issues.quote:
And the pressure did not stop there. The glacier kept advancing year after year. By the mid-seventeenth century, in some valleys the ice had almost sealed the passage shut.

issues.fix: The regional contrast raises the next question: what can the records establish about who suffered, and what remains uncertain about why?

issues.problem: 日本材料的具体数字与义仓机制未能核实，不能据此断言差异“不是天气”或由储粮制度造成。改后保留地区对照并限定其证明力。
issues.quote:
The answer is written in the registers.

In the 1780s and 1830s, when the Tenmei and Tenpō famines hit Japan, the records from northeastern villages show mortality and flight climbing together. In Hirosaki domain, the population loss approached half. Same sky, different archives. In the south, Kyushu records barely register the famines at all.

Same decades. Opposite outcomes. The difference was not weather.
issues.fix: The records show a sharp regional contrast. During the Tenmei famine of the 1780s and the Tenpō famine of the 1830s, northeastern village data show mortality and flight rising together. In Hirosaki domain, population loss approached half. Accounts from Kyushu contain little trace of famine deaths. These records establish different outcomes, not a single cause: climate, crops, trade, and local relief all matter to the comparison.

issues.problem: 原句宣称一地有储备与贸易、另一地没有，账本没有提供相应制度证据；也错误排除了纬度等变量。改为证据支持的有限结论。
issues.quote: The difference was not latitude. It was what had been organized before the cold arrived. One place had built reserves and trade networks in advance. Another had not.
issues.fix: Latitude and local conditions mattered. So did access to food and relief. The records here show that neighboring regions did not experience the famines in the same way, even though they do not let us isolate one cause.

issues.problem: 柯里里维尔具体死亡记录属于黑死病，不能作为小冰期饥荒死亡案例。保留heriot的方法论价值，同时清楚隔离其证据适用范围。
issues.quote:
The manor court at Curry Rivel in Somerset held sessions three times a year. Most of what it recorded was dull estate business: who violated the ale laws, who let a hedge fall, who owed the lord a day's plowing. In the sessions before 1348, the rolls list tenants by name for breaking regulations.

Then the rolls change.

Manor court rolls from Curry Rivel record deaths and heirs during 1348-1349, with heriot payments and inheritance listed. The steward wrote down who had died, what land they held, what was owed to the lord at death, and who inherited.
issues.fix: The manor court at Curry Rivel in Somerset recorded routine estate business as well as deaths and inheritances during 1348–1349. That record is useful for seeing how a heriot—a death duty owed to the lord—could identify a tenant and an heir. But those deaths belong to the Black Death, not to a climate-driven famine.

issues.problem: 原文把黑死病死亡率和庄园记录用于小冰期论证。改为明确区分两类灾害，并采用账本中的芬兰估算值。
issues.quote:
This is what makes counting possible. The manor court recorded deaths because the lord collected heriot — the death duty we saw at the start. A transaction between lord and heir, written into the rolls so the account would stand. That dull administrative obligation is what lets historians today count the households that did not make it through.

Multiply Curry Rivel across the parishes with surviving records. Historians studying the 1348-1350 epidemic have estimated mortality at one third to one half of the population in England.
issues.fix: That is how administrative records can help historians count people: a death duty, an inheritance, or an empty holding could leave a trace. But the Curry Rivel rolls cannot be used to count famine deaths. For a direct measure of a climate-related food crisis, the estimate for Finland's 1695–97 famine is that roughly one third of the population died.

issues.problem: 删除证据不足的拉基死亡人数，避免把不同口径的芬兰估算与日本地区记录并列成可直接比较的死亡账本。

issues.problem: 本章大段劳动力稀缺、限薪法令和农民起义的证据均属于黑死病人口冲击，不能证明小冰期的长期工资变化。替换为有边界的灾后判断，并保留原章向“村庄是否消失”转场的功能。
issues.quote:
The ground keeps its own calendar.

Spring 1350. The fields need plowing whether the village has enough hands or not. The seedtime does not wait for the parish to recover. And when the surviving families walked their strips that March, they walked past holdings no one had claimed. Fewer men sitting the benches in the manor court. Fewer carts on the road to market. Voices missing from the choir.

For the first time in living memory, the problem was not too many people and too little land.

It was the other way around.

The cost of getting work done flipped. Before the plague, a man holding a quarter-virgate worked his lord's strips two or three days a week as rent, and counted himself lucky to hold anything at all. After, the same man could look at twenty empty holdings and ask: what will you pay me to thresh your wheat?

The account rolls record the new arithmetic. Agricultural labor costs rose sharply after the Black Death. The work was the same. The grain was the same. The number of people able to swing a flail had dropped by a third or more, and every lord with a harvest needed them.

The crown knew it too.

In 1349, English authorities issued wage ordinances attempting to fix labor costs. Any labourer or artisan demanding more — named penalties. Any employer paying more — fined.

The account books show what happened.

The law named the rates. The shortage overrode them.

Fewer hands, same amount of land. Same fields to plow, same grain to thresh, same roofs to mend. Within five years, the lords who had legislated the wage ceiling were paying above it themselves, or watching their harvest rot.

And over the following decades, the structure began to shift. Labour services — the two or three days a week a tenant owed his lord — converted to cash rents. Tenants who had been tied to a holding by custom and law found the lord suddenly willing to negotiate. By the 1370s, villeins were bargaining. By the early 1380s, some were walking off holdings their families had worked for generations, because another manor down the road would pay more or ask less.

The long-term consequence was not immediate collapse. It was a slow loosening of the bonds that had held the manor system in place since before anyone could remember. Tenants who had inherited unfree status found the lord less interested in enforcing it when he needed hands. Courts that had once fined a villein for leaving without permission began letting it slide. Cash replaced obligation. Mobility replaced fixity.

And in June 1381, thirty years after the first plague summer, a tax revolt in Essex became a march on London, and the Peasants' Revolt burned the records in the Tower. The men who led it had grown up in the world the plague had left behind — a world where labour knew its value, and the law that said otherwise had already lost.

Everyone has heard that whole villages were simply wiped off the map. Is that what the records show?
issues.fix:
The ground keeps its own calendar. After a failed harvest, the next planting still had to happen on time. But the longer-term consequences of climate pressure were not the same as those of a sudden population collapse. The records here support a clearer change: during repeated shortages, communities faced the same urgent choices again and again—find food, draw on relief, or go without. That is why a single bad year and a long period of climatic stress should not be treated as the same kind of crisis.

And what about the claim that whole villages simply vanished?

issues.problem: 将格陵兰东部具体废弃年份改为账本支持的世纪范围，并避免把因纽特人的经历简化成“生活得很好”的笼统判断。
issues.quote:
But most places that emptied out didn't vanish in a season. The Norse Greenland colony's western settlement was abandoned around 1350, its eastern settlement sometime in the fifteenth century. It took generations. Sea ice closed the harbours. Pasture shrank. Trade lines died. The colony bled out slowly.

Meanwhile, the Inuit living in the same ice did well — kayaks, harpoons, sealskin clothing.
issues.fix: But many places that emptied out did not vanish in a season. Greenland's Norse settlements declined over time as sea ice, shrinking pasture, and disrupted trade made survival harder. The western settlement was abandoned around 1350; the eastern settlement lasted into the fifteenth century. Inuit subsistence systems, including kayaks, harpoons, and sealskin clothing, were better matched to the changing environment.

issues.problem: 删除属于黑死病语境且细节核验不足的阿什韦尔刻字；保留有来源的斯泰因格里姆松记录，并把熔岩停止的说法明确为当地传统。
issues.quote:
Records written about people. But what about words written by them?

Direct testimony from inside these years is rare. Most who lived through it left nothing. What survives is administrative — court rolls, tax lists, wills. But there are two exceptions.

In Ashwell, Hertfordshire, inside the tower of St Mary's church, someone carved words into the stone sometime between 1349 and 1350. Researchers describe the inscription as a determination not to let what happened be forgotten.

We don't know who held the chisel.

That's one voice, anonymous.

The other is named. In Iceland, a pastor named Jón Steingrímsson kept a day-by-day record through the 1783 Laki eruption — the same eruption that fed into the Tenmei famine. His account documents the sulphur haze, the livestock deaths, the famine that followed. Local tradition says his 'Fire Sermon' stopped the advancing lava at the village edge.
issues.fix: Records written about people are not the same as words written by them. Direct testimony from these years is rare. In Iceland, the pastor Jón Steingrímsson kept a day-by-day account during the 1783 Laki eruption, recording the eruption and its consequences. Local tradition says his “Fire Sermon” stopped the lava at the village edge, but the enduring evidence is the account he left behind.

issues.problem: 删除与小冰期无关的瘟疫回袭和缺乏明确来源的欧洲人口恢复时间；保留有依据的芬兰估算与1816年气候记录，明确回袭的时间尺度。
issues.quote:
And the cold years kept returning. The plague came back in repeated outbreaks through the 1360s and 1370s. Finland lost a third of its population in 1695 to 1697. The winter of 1709 froze Europe so hard that wine solidified in cellars and trees split open. In 1816, New York saw snow in June. Pennsylvania rivers froze in August.

Recovery took generations. The population levels of 1300 were not reached again until well into the sixteenth century.
issues.fix: The cold and harvest failures returned in different periods, rather than arriving as one continuous disaster. Finland's 1695–97 famine killed an estimated third of its population. In 1816, New York saw snow in June and Pennsylvania rivers froze in August. The evidence points to repeated shocks across centuries, not one uninterrupted famine or a single recovery timeline.

issues.problem: 苏格兰人口损失比例和达连计划具体投入、伤亡数字在终审核验中证据不足。改为不依赖这些数字的概括，并避免把合并归因于单一事件。
issues.quote: The bill was not only in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years, from 1695 to 1699, devastated the population. The famine drove a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. Scotland staked about a fifth of its national capital on a colony at the Panama isthmus. Three thousand settlers sailed in 1698. Two thousand died within two years. The scheme collapsed, and its failure put direct pressure on the 1707 union with England. One famine decade rewrote the constitutional map.
issues.fix: The cost was not only measured in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years coincided with a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. Scotland invested heavily in a colony at the Panama isthmus. The scheme failed, adding to the financial pressure that preceded the 1707 union with England. Famine and colonial failure formed part of a wider political crisis; neither alone explains the union.

issues.problem: 保留账本中树轮重建与明朝灭亡的时间信息，但删除由时间先后推导出的单一因果和反事实判断。
issues.quote: Other states missed the recovery window by years. Tree-ring reconstructions suggest temperatures returned toward historical averages by 1650. The Ming dynasty fell in 1644, six years before that threshold. The climatic pressure lifted just as the state gave way. Had the recovery come earlier, the outcome might have been different. But it did not.
issues.fix: Some tree-ring reconstructions place temperatures back near the historical average around 1650. The Ming dynasty fell in 1644. Climate was one of several pressures on the state, alongside political and military crises; the timing alone cannot show that an earlier climate recovery would have changed the outcome.

issues.problem: 原句将复杂的死亡差异归结为单一制度变量。改后保留组织和供给的重要性，同时避免绝对化。
issues.quote: The cold did not choose its victims at random. It killed where there was no system to interrupt the chain from harvest failure to starvation, and where there was no capital cushion to survive a failed bet.
issues.fix: The damage was not evenly distributed. It was greatest where failed harvests met limited reserves, weak trade, and little relief.

issues.problem: 逐问回应开场承诺，删除证据不足的法国禁种说和日本义仓因果断言，并避免把四个不同问题压成“只有一个答案”。
issues.quote: The four questions posted at the start turn out to have one answer. Cold became hunger when harvests failed and substitution ran out — the potato, banned in France until 1748 as pig food suspected of causing leprosy, was forced into the fields by Prussian famine policy in 1774 and became a northern staple. Who came through depended on whether reserves and trade were written down in advance: northeastern Japan's registers show mortality and flight climbing together in the 1780s Tenmei famine, while Kyushu in the south barely records it; Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. Neighbours under the same sky came out differently because provision was not evenly distributed. And what it left behind: England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure; the potato as insurance against grain failure; and in one Swiss village, a prayer against the glacier recited annually from the 1650s into the twentieth century, now approved by Rome in reverse — asking the ice to stay.
issues.fix: The four questions point to one larger lesson, but not one cause. First, cold and persistent rain damaged harvests, while crops and trade could ease the resulting shortage. Second, whether a household got through depended in part on what food and relief it could reach. Third, the Japanese records show sharply different regional outcomes, though they do not isolate why. Fourth, communities responded with measures such as potato cultivation, grain trade, and public provision. None made people immune to famine; each could change how far a shortage spread.

issues.problem: 删除瘟疫修士和紧急墓地的错误回扣，回到1315年春雨，并承认制度不能保证人人存活。
issues.quote: The friar in Messina wrote down a sickness clinging to bones. The households buried in that emergency ground were laid out head to foot, with care. The cold lasted from roughly the fourteenth century to the mid-nineteenth. The village carried on. Fields were plowed. Bells were rung. Harvests were recorded.
issues.fix: In the spring of 1315, the rain kept falling over fields that needed to be planted. The record of the famine does not promise that every household survived. It shows why the harvest, the market, and whatever relief a community could organize all mattered.

issues.problem: 原结论否定了纬度与天气的作用，也把制度说成唯一答案。改后兼顾气候风险与组织能力，并以明确判断收尾。
issues.quote: The comfort of knowing why crops fail and having reserves written into law is strikingly new. For most of history, what helped people survive was never luck or a warmer latitude. It was the system someone had built before the cold arrived.
issues.fix: Modern food systems can explain crop failures and plan reserves in advance. Latitude and weather still mattered in the Little Ice Age. But when harvests failed, access to food and relief shaped how far the crisis spread. The rain created the crisis; what a community had prepared helped determine its reach.

issues.problem: 原文把中文引文直接译成生硬英文，听觉不自然。改为简洁转述，并保留地方志引述这一来源限定。
issues.quote: In 1639, a county gazetteer in Shandong recorded: "From first month no rain to sixth month, seventh month great locusts, the year greatly hungry, people ate people, wanderers filled the roads."
issues.fix: A 1639 Shandong county gazetteer recorded a severe drought, locusts, famine, and people fleeing their homes.

issues.problem: 原句容易被听成所有人都活了下来，且“组织”近似唯一原因。改后承认幸存范围有限，并与结尾因果边界一致。
issues.quote: They survived by organising before the crisis arrived.
issues.fix: Some survived because their communities had organized before the crisis arrived.

edits.old:
October 1347, the start of the Little Ice Age. A harbour in Sicily, late autumn. Twelve Genoese galleys tying up at Messina after a long run from the east. A Franciscan friar in the town writes down one line about the men coming ashore.

They had brought with them a sickness clinging to their very bones.

He does not explain the phrase. He cannot. Within a year it will have travelled every trade road in Europe. For the next five hundred years, survival itself became the question. Everything that followed was written down. Not legend — records.

But this is not a film about that harbour.
edits.new: Spring 1315. In northern Europe, the rain began and kept falling. Fields turned to mud. Grain prices rose as harvests failed. This was the start of a famine that would expose a harder question: when cold and rain threaten the harvest, what helps a household survive? The answer is recorded in court rolls, grain prices, tree rings, and the abandoned places left behind.
edits.reason: 原开场把黑死病抵达墨西拿误写成小冰期开始，也让观众误以为主题是瘟疫。改用1315年饥荒开场，直接点出标题冲突，并提前给出史料与核心问题。

edits.old: In the manor court rolls that tracked every tenant's death. In the tree rings that measured each growing season. In the emergency burial grounds archaeologists dug up centuries later.
edits.new: In manor court rolls that recorded tenants and inheritances. In tree rings that measured growing seasons. In grain prices and the remains of places abandoned as conditions changed.
edits.reason: 紧急墓地主要是瘟疫证据，不适合作为小冰期的核心证据。替换为与饥荒和气候变化相关的记录与遗迹。

edits.old:
That question splits into four.

First: how does cold turn into famine — and what interrupts that chain? A growing season shortens by a week or two — where does the hunger actually start?

Second: when harvests fail, what decides who survives? Luck, or something written down in advance?

Third: why do neighbouring places, under the same sky, come out so differently? One village loses a few families. Another loses half its population. What separates them?

Fourth: what did surviving communities build that others did not? In the economy. In the law. In the way people thought about survival itself.
edits.new:
That question splits into four.

First, in the famine chain: how does bad weather become hunger, and what can interrupt it?

Second, when harvests fail, what helps a household get through: luck, or support already in place?

Third, why do nearby regions sometimes suffer differently under the same broad climate pressures?

And fourth, what did communities build that helped them face the next shortage?
edits.reason: 保留四问，但删去缺乏核实的“一个村庄损失一半”预设，并明确四问对应后文的饥荒链条、应对、地区差异和制度遗产。

edits.old: So how long did this cold period last, how cold was it, and what did the world look like before it arrived?
edits.new: To answer those questions, start with the period's scale and the pressures people already faced.
edits.reason: 原句重复追问寒冷的时间与幅度，下一章马上会解释背景；改后直接引入灾前基线。

edits.old: The Little Ice Age cooled the northern hemisphere by under one degree Celsius. Tree rings and ice cores measure the drop by reading volcanic eruptions and solar output. Four volcanic eruptions before the cold began: the 1257 Samalas eruption, magnitude seven on the volcanic explosivity index, followed by three more between 1268 and 1284, then another in the 1450s. Each threw sulphur into the stratosphere, reflecting sunlight back to space. Then four solar minima stretched across the centuries: the Wolf minimum, the Spörer, the Maunder minimum from 1645 to 1715, and the Dalton. Decades when sunspot counts dropped and solar output weakened.
edits.new: The Little Ice Age cooled the northern hemisphere by under one degree Celsius. Tree rings and ice cores help reconstruct the climate. Major volcanic eruptions, including Samalas in 1257 and another in the 1450s, pushed conditions colder by sending sulphur into the atmosphere, where it reflected sunlight. Several periods of low solar activity also stretched across these centuries, including the Maunder minimum from 1645 to 1715.

edits.old: They blamed the stars. The University of Paris in 1348 issued a formal explanation: a conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars in Aquarius in the 1340s had drawn poisonous vapour from the earth and corrupted the air. The Church added divine punishment. Processions, prayer, fasting. Someone had to be at fault. In the coldest decades, accusations found targets.
edits.new: People explained disaster through the ideas available to them: celestial events, corrupted air, or divine punishment. Those explanations tell us how people made sense of crisis, but they do not establish what caused the Little Ice Age.
edits.reason: 原段把1348年的瘟疫解释移入小冰期叙事，并暗示寒冷年代的指控机制。改为不依赖瘟疫材料的时代认知说明。

edits.old:
What isn't disputed is that the cold arrived along routes the village already used.

The weekly market. The church court. The mill where grain was ground. Roads the priest walked, the miller's cart followed, the lord's steward travelled when collecting rents. The harbour that brought salt and wool and carried grain away. The village was not sealed off. Its survival required connection.
edits.new: What traveled along those routes was the shortage: market prices, grain supplies, and news of failed harvests. A village was not sealed off. Its survival could depend on the market, the mill, and the roads that connected it to other sources of food.
edits.reason: 寒冷不会沿道路传播，原句沿用了瘟疫传播的比喻。改为说明道路和市场传播的是粮食短缺与供给信息。

edits.old:
In the winter of 1683 to 1684, the Thames froze solid for two months. Londoners built two streets of shops on the river: taverns, roast ox, bear-baiting. King Charles and his queen shared a portion. A printer set up a press on the ice, selling cards for sixpence with your name and the date. One printer took in five pounds a day. The diarist John Evelyn called it a Bacchanalian triumph on the river while on land it was severe judgment.

On January 23rd, 1795, the sea off Den Helder froze. A column of French hussars wrapped their horses' hooves in cloth, rode across the ice, and captured fourteen Dutch warships without firing a shot. Cavalry took a fleet.

The cold could reach that far.
edits.new: In the winter of 1683 to 1684, the Thames froze for about two months. Londoners built two streets of shops on the river. The diarist John Evelyn described the contrast: celebration on the ice, severe hardship on land. In 1795, French cavalry rode across frozen water near Den Helder and captured fourteen Dutch warships. These episodes show how severe the cold could be, but the question here is what happened when it reached the harvest.
edits.reason: 保留两项有依据的寒冷例证和伊夫林的对照，删除未经核实的冰层厚度、收入等细节，并明确奇观如何回到饥荒主线。

edits.old:
And people tried to stop it. In the Chamonix valley, one Swiss village began an annual procession in the 1650s, walking up the mountain to pray that the glacier would not swallow their pastures. Every year for three centuries they asked.

The glacier advanced anyway. From 1641 to 1643, the Bois glacier moved forward seventy-five to one hundred and fifty meters every year, nearly closing the valley.

It didn't work. Not because the villagers lacked effort or faith, but because what was arriving moved on a scale no procession could deflect.
edits.new: In the Chamonix valley, villagers began an annual procession in the 1650s, praying that the glacier would spare their pastures. The Bois glacier advanced anyway: from 1641 to 1643, it moved forward seventy-five to one hundred and fifty meters a year, nearly closing the valley. Prayer could not stop the ice, but this was only one part of survival. A household also had to get through the winter indoors.
edits.reason: 压缩重复的祈祷与“没有成功”表述，保留有来源的冰川推进事实，并将段落自然转入居住与取暖。

edits.old:
The house itself was timber frame with wattle-and-daub walls and a thatched roof. Most of the heat left through the walls and the thatch. An open hearth in the centre burned what wood the family could gather, but without a closed firebox most of the warmth went straight out through the roof.

Where fuel was abundant and building traditions different, the problem had been solved centuries earlier. In German-speaking regions and Scandinavia, the kachelofen — a tiled masonry stove — routed smoke through a maze of internal channels, holding the heat long after the fire went out. Two hours of burning gave ten to twelve hours of warmth. By the eighteenth century, wood shortages were severe enough that several governments funded improvements to stove design.

In Russia, the stove itself was the bed. Families built brick structures weighing over a ton, routing the smoke horizontally through a knee-shaped flue, and slept on top of it through the winter.

The English household in this film had none of that. They closed off most of the house for the season and lived in the kitchen. They hung curtains around the bed to trap body heat. They filled a long-handled copper warming pan with coals from the hearth and ran it between the sheets before climbing in. They wrapped heated stones and soapstone in cloth and kept them at their feet. At church, they brought their own foot stoves to survive the hour-long sermon. And they slept together — the entire household in one bed.

Heat you can arrange yourself. Food you cannot. When the harvest failed, who was supposed to feed this family?
edits.new:
Homes varied. In German-speaking regions, tiled masonry stoves held heat after the fire went out; in Russia, families slept on top of the central stove. The English household in this example had neither advantage. It closed off most of the house, lived in the kitchen, and used bed curtains and warmed stones to conserve heat.

But warmth could not replace food. When the harvest failed, who was supposed to feed the family?
edits.reason: 取暖技术段落占篇幅过多，且炉具效率等细节证据不足。压缩为地区对比与普通家庭的应对，并把重点交回粮食问题。

edits.old: Largely no one. There was no state granary, no central relief, no assured supply. The answer was substitution — in the field and on the plate.
edits.new: For many households, no reliable supply was guaranteed. One answer was substitution — in the field and on the plate.
edits.reason: 原句把没有粮仓、救济和供给说成普遍事实，过于绝对。改为限定普通家庭面对的供给不确定性。

edits.old: The crop that eventually underwrote northern diets had arrived in Europe in the mid-1500s and spent two centuries despised. The potato was pig food. France banned it outright in 1748 on suspicion it caused leprosy. What changed was famine. In 1744, Frederick the Great of Prussia issued it as military rations. In 1774, famine year, he ordered it planted across the kingdom and distributed free seed.
edits.new: The potato arrived in Europe in the mid-1500s and faced long resistance. Famine helped change its status. In 1744, Frederick the Great of Prussia issued it as military rations. During the famine of 1774, he ordered it planted across the kingdom and distributed free seed.
edits.reason: 事实核验将法国1748年禁种说列为证据不足。删除该具体断言，保留账本支持的土豆推广过程。

edits.old:
In Finland during the 1695–97 famine, that meant bark bread and wild ferns.

One of these worked. The other was just hunger with a recipe.
edits.new: In Finland during the 1695–97 famine, people ate bark bread and wild ferns. Neither could replace grain; both were emergency foods people turned to when ordinary supplies failed.
edits.reason: 原句没有证据判断哪种食物有效，后一句也没有说明判断依据。改为只陈述账本支持的食用情况及其不能替代谷物的作用。

edits.old: Where institutions held, the picture was different. Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged — its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure, built provision into statute before the next round arrived. In Japan's Tenmei famine of the 1780s, domains with community grain stores saw lower mortality than those without.

Researchers read England's 1598 Poor Law as an institutional response to climate pressure. The Japanese records show sharply different regional outcomes during the Tenmei famine; they do not, by themselves, establish how a particular grain-store system worked.
edits.reason: 保留账本支持的贸易和济贫法材料，将日本地区结果与未经证实的义仓因果机制分开，避免把相关性说成已证实的制度效果。

edits.old:
The pressure kept building into 1349. Substitution had bought a few months. By that winter, the pressure had reached the institutions themselves — and the paperwork.

In 1349, Pope Clement VI issued directives concerning the last rite no one could do without: confession and absolution.

Under normal canon law, a dying person confessed to an ordained priest. Only a priest could grant absolution. The directive changed that. A plague victim facing death could now confess to any qualified confessor and receive absolution of all sins. That included laypeople — men with no ordination. If no man was available, it allowed confession to a woman.

This is not a chronicle entry or a local bishop's improvisation. This is the papacy adjusting the procedure for the soul's final passage and putting the adjustment on paper during the emergency.

It is a rare thing to find an institution bending a rule this central. Rarer still to find it done in writing as if the institution could budget for catastrophe the way it budgeted for jubilees.

The directive traveled through the dioceses. The Archbishop of York forwarded it to the Bishop of Carlisle and others. The rule had changed on paper.

If the rules broke down on paper, everything on the ground must have broken down too. Did it?
edits.new: The question now moves from emergency food to lasting provision. In England, researchers interpret the 1598 Poor Law as one institutional response to climate pressure: support was written into law rather than left entirely to a household's luck. That does not mean relief could prevent every death. It means a community could make provision before the next shortage arrived.
edits.reason: 原段教皇教令、告解与瘟疫压力均不属于小冰期饥荒论证。改用账本中的济贫法研究解读，承接替代食物与制度性应对。

edits.old:
If the rules broke down on paper, you would expect the ground to give way completely. Bodies left where they fell. Households scattering without record. The kind of collapse that leaves no trace beyond the silence itself.

That is not what the excavations show.

Emergency burial grounds excavated in England from the plague years held organized burials. In one cemetery, researchers found individuals still laid out head-to-foot in consistent alignment, as if the calendar had kept its ordinary shape even when nothing else did.

What caught the researchers was not the number. It was the arrangement.

Even under that much pressure, someone had taken the time to do it properly. The dead were not piled or abandoned. They were buried as neighbours, with the kind of care that does not show up in the death toll but says something about the people who kept going.
edits.new: But a written policy is not the same as food in a household's hands. The Japanese records give us a different kind of comparison: during the Tenmei and Tenpō famines, northeastern records show mortality and flight rising together, while accounts from Kyushu contain little trace of famine deaths. The contrast matters, but it does not tell us on its own which local institutions produced it.
edits.reason: 原段用黑死病墓地考古证明小冰期时期的照护与秩序，证据错配。改为现有日本地区记录，并明确其不能单独证明具体制度因果。

edits.old:
And the pressure did not stop there. The glacier kept advancing year after year. By the mid-seventeenth century, in some valleys the ice had almost sealed the passage shut.

If people under that much pressure stayed capable of care, then what made the difference between a village that lost a few and a village that lost half?
edits.new: The regional contrast raises the next question: what can the records establish about who suffered, and what remains uncertain about why?
edits.reason: 原文继续用冰川和瘟疫式“照护反转”延伸不相关论证。改后承接日本对照，明确进入证据与因果边界。

edits.old:
The answer is written in the registers.

In the 1780s and 1830s, when the Tenmei and Tenpō famines hit Japan, the records from northeastern villages show mortality and flight climbing together. In Hirosaki domain, the population loss approached half. Same sky, different archives. In the south, Kyushu records barely register the famines at all.

Same decades. Opposite outcomes. The difference was not weather.

In Hirosaki domain, population loss approached half. Accounts from Kyushu contain little trace of famine deaths. These records establish different outcomes, not a single cause: climate, crops, trade, and local relief all matter to the comparison.
edits.reason: 日本材料的具体数字与义仓机制未能核实，不能据此断言差异“不是天气”或由储粮制度造成。改后保留地区对照并限定其证明力。

edits.old: The difference was not latitude. It was what had been organized before the cold arrived. One place had built reserves and trade networks in advance. Another had not.
edits.new: Latitude and local conditions mattered. So did access to food and relief. The records here show that neighboring regions did not experience the famines in the same way, even though they do not let us isolate one cause.
edits.reason: 原句宣称一地有储备与贸易、另一地没有，账本没有提供相应制度证据；也错误排除了纬度等变量。改为证据支持的有限结论。

edits.old:
The manor court at Curry Rivel in Somerset held sessions three times a year. Most of what it recorded was dull estate business: who violated the ale laws, who let a hedge fall, who owed the lord a day's plowing. In the sessions before 1348, the rolls list tenants by name for breaking regulations.

Then the rolls change.

Manor court rolls from Curry Rivel record deaths and heirs during 1348-1349, with heriot payments and inheritance listed. The steward wrote down who had died, what land they held, what was owed to the lord at death, and who inherited.
edits.new: The manor court at Curry Rivel in Somerset recorded routine estate business as well as deaths and inheritances during 1348–1349. That record is useful for seeing how a heriot—a death duty owed to the lord—could identify a tenant and an heir. But those deaths belong to the Black Death, not to a climate-driven famine.
edits.reason: 柯里里维尔具体死亡记录属于黑死病，不能作为小冰期饥荒死亡案例。保留heriot的方法论价值，同时清楚隔离其证据适用范围。

edits.old:
This is what makes counting possible. The manor court recorded deaths because the lord collected heriot — the death duty we saw at the start. A transaction between lord and heir, written into the rolls so the account would stand. That dull administrative obligation is what lets historians today count the households that did not make it through.

Multiply Curry Rivel across the parishes with surviving records. Historians studying the 1348-1350 epidemic have estimated mortality at one third to one half of the population in England.
edits.new: That is how administrative records can help historians count people: a death duty, an inheritance, or an empty holding could leave a trace. But the Curry Rivel rolls cannot be used to count famine deaths. For a direct measure of a climate-related food crisis, the estimate for Finland's 1695–97 famine is that roughly one third of the population died.
edits.reason: 原文把黑死病死亡率和庄园记录用于小冰期论证。改为明确区分两类灾害，并采用账本中的芬兰估算值。

edits.old: The coldest stretches killed in different measures. Finland's 1695-97 famine is estimated to have taken roughly one third of the population. Iceland's Laki eruption in 1783 and the famine that followed took a heavy toll. Japan's Tenmei famine cost Hirosaki domain nearly half.
edits.new: In Finland's 1695–97 famine, an estimated one third of the population died. In Japan, the Tenmei-era records show severe population loss in Hirosaki and little trace of famine deaths in Kyushu. These figures and records do not share one measurement method, so they should not be treated as a single comparable death toll.
edits.reason: 删除证据不足的拉基死亡人数，避免把不同口径的芬兰估算与日本地区记录并列成可直接比较的死亡账本。

edits.old:
The ground keeps its own calendar.

Spring 1350. The fields need plowing whether the village has enough hands or not. The seedtime does not wait for the parish to recover. And when the surviving families walked their strips that March, they walked past holdings no one had claimed. Fewer men sitting the benches in the manor court. Fewer carts on the road to market. Voices missing from the choir.

For the first time in living memory, the problem was not too many people and too little land.

It was the other way around.

The cost of getting work done flipped. Before the plague, a man holding a quarter-virgate worked his lord's strips two or three days a week as rent, and counted himself lucky to hold anything at all. After, the same man could look at twenty empty holdings and ask: what will you pay me to thresh your wheat?

The account rolls record the new arithmetic. Agricultural labor costs rose sharply after the Black Death. The work was the same. The grain was the same. The number of people able to swing a flail had dropped by a third or more, and every lord with a harvest needed them.

The crown knew it too.

In 1349, English authorities issued wage ordinances attempting to fix labor costs. Any labourer or artisan demanding more — named penalties. Any employer paying more — fined.

The account books show what happened.

The law named the rates. The shortage overrode them.

Fewer hands, same amount of land. Same fields to plow, same grain to thresh, same roofs to mend. Within five years, the lords who had legislated the wage ceiling were paying above it themselves, or watching their harvest rot.

And over the following decades, the structure began to shift. Labour services — the two or three days a week a tenant owed his lord — converted to cash rents. Tenants who had been tied to a holding by custom and law found the lord suddenly willing to negotiate. By the 1370s, villeins were bargaining. By the early 1380s, some were walking off holdings their families had worked for generations, because another manor down the road would pay more or ask less.

The long-term consequence was not immediate collapse. It was a slow loosening of the bonds that had held the manor system in place since before anyone could remember. Tenants who had inherited unfree status found the lord less interested in enforcing it when he needed hands. Courts that had once fined a villein for leaving without permission began letting it slide. Cash replaced obligation. Mobility replaced fixity.

And in June 1381, thirty years after the first plague summer, a tax revolt in Essex became a march on London, and the Peasants' Revolt burned the records in the Tower. The men who led it had grown up in the world the plague had left behind — a world where labour knew its value, and the law that said otherwise had already lost.

Everyone has heard that whole villages were simply wiped off the map. Is that what the records show?
edits.new:
The ground keeps its own calendar. After a failed harvest, the next planting still had to happen on time. But the longer-term consequences of climate pressure were not the same as those of a sudden population collapse. The records here support a clearer change: during repeated shortages, communities faced the same urgent choices again and again—find food, draw on relief, or go without. That is why a single bad year and a long period of climatic stress should not be treated as the same kind of crisis.

And what about the claim that whole villages simply vanished?
edits.reason: 本章大段劳动力稀缺、限薪法令和农民起义的证据均属于黑死病人口冲击，不能证明小冰期的长期工资变化。替换为有边界的灾后判断，并保留原章向“村庄是否消失”转场的功能。

edits.old:
But most places that emptied out didn't vanish in a season. The Norse Greenland colony's western settlement was abandoned around 1350, its eastern settlement sometime in the fifteenth century. It took generations. Sea ice closed the harbours. Pasture shrank. Trade lines died. The colony bled out slowly.

Meanwhile, the Inuit living in the same ice did well — kayaks, harpoons, sealskin clothing.
edits.new: But many places that emptied out did not vanish in a season. Greenland's Norse settlements declined over time as sea ice, shrinking pasture, and disrupted trade made survival harder. The western settlement was abandoned around 1350; the eastern settlement lasted into the fifteenth century. Inuit subsistence systems, including kayaks, harpoons, and sealskin clothing, were better matched to the changing environment.
edits.reason: 将格陵兰东部具体废弃年份改为账本支持的世纪范围，并避免把因纽特人的经历简化成“生活得很好”的笼统判断。

edits.old:
Records written about people. But what about words written by them?

Direct testimony from inside these years is rare. Most who lived through it left nothing. What survives is administrative — court rolls, tax lists, wills. But there are two exceptions.

In Ashwell, Hertfordshire, inside the tower of St Mary's church, someone carved words into the stone sometime between 1349 and 1350. Researchers describe the inscription as a determination not to let what happened be forgotten.

We don't know who held the chisel.

That's one voice, anonymous.

The other is named. In Iceland, a pastor named Jón Steingrímsson kept a day-by-day record through the 1783 Laki eruption — the same eruption that fed into the Tenmei famine. His account documents the sulphur haze, the livestock deaths, the famine that followed. Local tradition says his 'Fire Sermon' stopped the advancing lava at the village edge.
edits.new: Records written about people are not the same as words written by them. Direct testimony from these years is rare. In Iceland, the pastor Jón Steingrímsson kept a day-by-day account during the 1783 Laki eruption, recording the eruption and its consequences. Local tradition says his “Fire Sermon” stopped the lava at the village edge, but the enduring evidence is the account he left behind.
edits.reason: 删除属于黑死病语境且细节核验不足的阿什韦尔刻字；保留有来源的斯泰因格里姆松记录，并把熔岩停止的说法明确为当地传统。

edits.old:
And the cold years kept returning. The plague came back in repeated outbreaks through the 1360s and 1370s. Finland lost a third of its population in 1695 to 1697. The winter of 1709 froze Europe so hard that wine solidified in cellars and trees split open. In 1816, New York saw snow in June. Pennsylvania rivers froze in August.

Recovery took generations. The population levels of 1300 were not reached again until well into the sixteenth century.

In 1816, New York saw snow in June and Pennsylvania rivers froze in August. The evidence points to repeated shocks across centuries, not one uninterrupted famine or a single recovery timeline.

edits.old: The bill was not only in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years, from 1695 to 1699, devastated the population. The famine drove a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. Scotland staked about a fifth of its national capital on a colony at the Panama isthmus. Three thousand settlers sailed in 1698. Two thousand died within two years. The scheme collapsed, and its failure put direct pressure on the 1707 union with England. One famine decade rewrote the constitutional map.
edits.new: The cost was not only measured in lives. Scotland's Seven Ill Years coincided with a desperate venture: the Darien scheme. Scotland invested heavily in a colony at the Panama isthmus. The scheme failed, adding to the financial pressure that preceded the 1707 union with England. Famine and colonial failure formed part of a wider political crisis; neither alone explains the union.

The Ming dynasty fell in 1644, six years before that threshold. The climatic pressure lifted just as the state gave way. Had the recovery come earlier, the outcome might have been different. But it did not.

Climate was one of several pressures on the state, alongside political and military crises; the timing alone cannot show that an earlier climate recovery would have changed the outcome.
edits.reason: 保留账本中树轮重建与明朝灭亡的时间信息，但删除由时间先后推导出的单一因果和反事实判断。

edits.old: The cold did not choose its victims at random. It killed where there was no system to interrupt the chain from harvest failure to starvation, and where there was no capital cushion to survive a failed bet.
edits.new: The damage was not evenly distributed. It was greatest where failed harvests met limited reserves, weak trade, and little relief.
edits.reason: 原句将复杂的死亡差异归结为单一制度变量。改后保留组织和供给的重要性，同时避免绝对化。

edits.old: The four questions posted at the start turn out to have one answer. Cold became hunger when harvests failed and substitution ran out — the potato, banned in France until 1748 as pig food suspected of causing leprosy, was forced into the fields by Prussian famine policy in 1774 and became a northern staple. Who came through depended on whether reserves and trade were written down in advance: northeastern Japan's registers show mortality and flight climbing together in the 1780s Tenmei famine, while Kyushu in the south barely records it; Amsterdam came through the 1590s continent-wide famine least damaged because its Baltic grain trade kept supply flowing. Neighbours under the same sky came out differently because provision was not evenly distributed. And what it left behind: England's 1598 Poor Law, read by researchers as written adaptation to climate pressure; the potato as insurance against grain failure; and in one Swiss village, a prayer against the glacier recited annually from the 1650s into the twentieth century, now approved by Rome in reverse — asking the ice to stay.
edits.new: The four questions point to one larger lesson, but not one cause. First, cold and persistent rain damaged harvests, while crops and trade could ease the resulting shortage. Second, whether a household got through depended in part on what food and relief it could reach. Third, the Japanese records show sharply different regional outcomes, though they do not isolate why. Fourth, communities responded with measures such as potato cultivation, grain trade, and public provision. None made people immune to famine; each could change how far a shortage spread.

edits.old: The friar in Messina wrote down a sickness clinging to bones. The households buried in that emergency ground were laid out head to foot, with care. The cold lasted from roughly the fourteenth century to the mid-nineteenth. The village carried on. Fields were plowed. Bells were rung. Harvests were recorded.

edits.old: The comfort of knowing why crops fail and having reserves written into law is strikingly new. For most of history, what helped people survive was never luck or a warmer latitude. It was the system someone had built before the cold arrived.
edits.new: Modern food systems can explain crop failures and plan reserves in advance. Latitude and weather still mattered in the Little Ice Age. But when harvests failed, access to food and relief shaped how far the crisis spread. The rain created the crisis; what a community had prepared helped determine its reach.
